title: The Ninth Bell of the Meridian Gull
author: Marisol Quint
description: Twenty-four chapters aboard a sky-ferry that stays in the air because nine bells are rung in the right order, at the right hour, by people who have not slept. Sol Ferrant is sixteen, has the best ear on the ship, and is the only person willing to say out loud that the ninth bell has started answering someone else. chapters.title: Chapter One: The Note Under the Note

blocks.c: Chapter One: The Note Under the Note
The third watch belonged to Sol Ferrant, and the third watch belonged to nobody, which was much the same thing.

She climbed the bell ladder at ten minutes to four with the rope callus on her right palm itching the way it always did before a round, and she counted the rungs, because counting was free. Nineteen rungs from the galley deck to the ring gallery. Nineteen going up, nineteen coming down, and in between, nine bells and four hundred and eleven passengers who had paid good Antrell silver to be carried across a sea made of weather.

The Meridian Gull was a ring-ship, which meant it did not fly so much as agree not to fall. Sol had explained this to exactly one passenger in her three years aboard, a boy of about nine who had asked with the terrible seriousness of the very young what held the ship up, and she had said: sound does. He had asked what happened if the sound stopped. She had said, we ring it again before it stops. He had considered this, nodded once, and gone to be sick over the rail, which she felt was a fair response to the situation.

The gallery ran the length of the spine, open to the wind on both sides, with the nine bells hung in their cradles down the middle like a row of iron hearts. They had names because everything on a ring-ship had a name; a thing with no name cannot be shouted for in a storm.
Keel, at the bow, deepest and slowest.
Then Ladder. Then Kestrel, then Quarrel, then Mother, who was the biggest and had a voice like a landslide being polite. Then Lantern, Thimble, Widow.
And at the stern, small and high and bright, the Ninth. The Gull. The bell the ship was named for, or the other way round; nobody living remembered which and everyone had an opinion.

Sol touched each cradle as she walked the line. That was not procedure. That was superstition, and she knew it was superstition, and she did it anyway, the same way her hand found the rail on a stair in the dark.

The round is nine strikes in a fixed order, at a fixed interval, once every watch. That is the whole of it and it takes eleven minutes and any child of Kettlemouth can recite the order before they can spell their own name.
What no child of Kettlemouth can do is hear whether it worked.

The strike itself is nothing. Anyone can swing a hammer. What matters is what the bell does afterward, in the long tail of the sound, when the note has gone quiet enough that the passengers stop noticing it and the ship starts. The bell-hands call it the underhum. It sits below hearing, in the teeth and the sternum, and it is the underhum that the ship stands on, and a bell that strikes bright and hums thin is a bell that is lying to you.

Sol had the best ear on the Gull. She knew this without vanity, the way she knew she was short. Bosun Roake had told her so once, in the flat voice she used for weather reports and disappointments, and had then made her scrub the gallery for a week to remove any pleasure from the compliment.
She set her feet. She took the hammer from its hook. And she rang the round.
Keel, low and enormous, the sound going out and down and out again.
Ladder, four beats later. Kestrel. Quarrel. Mother, who took a full breath to decide to speak and then said everything at once. Lantern. Thimble. Widow, sour and reliable.
Sol walked the last six paces to the stern in the dark with the whole ship humming under her boots, and she lifted the hammer to the Ninth, and she struck it, and it rang beautifully.
And then it did not hum.
She stood there for the length of four heartbeats with the hammer still up, listening to a silence that had no business existing.

Not a thin hum. Not a flat one. Nothing. The bell had made a lovely bright noise and then it had simply stopped, the way a bell will if you clap your hand on it, except nobody had clapped a hand on it, and there was nothing on the gallery but Sol and the wind and four hundred and eleven sleeping people underneath her feet.
She struck it again, which was against every rule Roake had ever driven into her, because a bell struck out of round is a bell arguing with itself.
It rang. It went quiet.

The third time, the underhum came back — late, arriving a half-beat after it should have, faint and strange, and Sol felt it in her sternum and knew at once, with a certainty she would spend eleven weeks trying to explain to people who did not want it explained, that she was not feeling the Ninth.
She was feeling something else answering on the Ninth's behalf. From a long way off. From below.
The deck tilted.

It was a small tilt, the kind that makes a mug slide two inches and stop, the kind that a passenger sleeps through and a crewman does not. Somewhere below her a loose crate went over with a sound like a dropped argument, and the Gull dipped her nose, and the horizon of cloud came up half a span and settled again as the eight good bells took the weight.
Half a span. It is nothing. A ring-ship carries forty.

Sol Ferrant stood in the wind at the stern of the ring gallery with the hammer in her hand and her heart going like a bird in a box, and she looked at the small bright bell that the whole ship was named for, and she said, out loud, to nobody:
"That wasn't you, was it."
The Ninth, being iron, declined to comment.

chapters.title: Chapter Two: Nine Names, One Round

blocks.c: Chapter Two: Nine Names, One Round
Bosun Tamsin Roake had been bell-master of the Meridian Gull for twenty-two years, and the first thing she said, every time, without exception, was: "Was it in the tally?"
"Not yet," said Sol.
"Then it did not happen."
"It happened."

"Then write it in the tally, and then it will have happened, and then I will care about it." Roake did not look up. She was doing what she was always doing at half past four in the morning, which was sitting in the bell-master's cubby with a lamp turned down to a coin of light, splicing a hammer-lanyard with hands that had been broken often enough to have opinions about weather. "Sit down. You're dripping."
Sol sat. The cubby was the size of a coffin stood on end and smelled of tallow, iron filings and the particular sourness of a woman who had not been ashore in six weeks.
She wrote it in the tally.

The tally was a ledger as long as her forearm and as thick as her fist, ruled in columns by some Antrell clerk a century ago, and every round rung on the Gull since had a line in it: the watch, the hand who rang it, the nine bells in order, and beside each bell a mark for the hum. Full. Thin. Dead. Nine marks, four times a day, every day, for as long as the ship had been in the air. Sol had once worked out that there were more than a hundred and twenty thousand lines in the tally and had immediately wished she had not, because a number like that sits on you.
She wrote: Third watch. Ferrant. Keel full, Ladder full, Kestrel full, Quarrel full, Mother full, Lantern full, Thimble full, Widow full.
Her pen stopped over the ninth column.
"There isn't a mark for it," she said.
"There's three marks. Full, thin, dead."
"It wasn't any of those. It rang and there was nothing and then something came back late and it wasn't ours."

Roake's hands stopped moving on the lanyard. It was such a small thing that Sol nearly missed it. Then the hands started again, and the bosun said, in the voice she used for weather, "Mark it dead. Add a note in the margin. Margins are free."
Here is what Sol knew about the round, because it had been beaten into her the way a shape is beaten into hot iron, which is to say slowly and with a great deal of noise.

items: Nine bells, in order, bow to stern. Never out of order. A round rung backwards has been tried twice in recorded history and the second time was to see whether the first time had been a coincidence.
Four beats between strikes, counted by the hand, not by any device. Devices go wrong quietly. Hands go wrong loudly, and a bell-hand who has lost the count will say so, if she was raised right.

The round is rung four times a day, at the turn of each watch, and the carry it lays down lasts a little more than eight hours, which gives you slack. The slack is not spare. The slack is the reason anyone is alive.

If a bell hums thin, ring the round again. If a bell hums dead, ring the round again and send for the bell-master. If two hum dead in the same round, the bell-master sends for the captain, and the captain begins to think about where the ground is.
You do not ring a bell out of round. Ever. A bell struck alone is a bell with nothing to lean on.

blocks.c: Sol had broken the last of those an hour ago, twice, and had put both strikes in the tally, in the margin, in her smallest handwriting, because Roake was right that margins were free but she was not going to pretend they were invisible.
"Tell me about your ear," said Roake.
"You've heard about my ear."
"Tell me anyway. Humour an old woman, and if you say I'm not old I'll put you on ballast."

Sol looked at the coin of lamplight. "I hear the tail. Everyone hears the strike. The strike is loud, the strike is the part passengers clap for. I hear what's under it, and I can tell you if it's ours."
"Ours."

"Every bell has a voice. Not a pitch — a voice. Mother's is like something big turning over in its sleep. Widow sounds like she's already decided you're wrong." She turned the pen over in her fingers. "The Ninth sounds like someone answering a question politely."

Roake was quiet for a while. On the far side of the bulkhead the ship made all the small sounds a ring-ship makes: the sigh of the lift-frames taking the carry, the tick of cooling iron, the distant argument of two cooks.
"I was fourteen when I first heard a bell answer wrong," said Roake. "Nobody believed me either. Do you know what I did about it?"
"What?"
"Nothing. For eleven years." She bit the lanyard's end off with her back teeth. "Do better than that."

Sol Ferrant had come aboard the Gull at thirteen, out of Kettlemouth, where the cloud comes down to the harbour wall and the whole town smells of tar and cold iron. Her mother had been a ropewalker in the yards. Her father was a rumour with a good singing voice. Neither fact had ever been of much practical use except that she had grown up around ropes and around singing, and it turns out that if you want to make a bell-hand, ropes and singing is most of the recipe.
The rest of the recipe is the tally, and the tally is the reason bell-hands are strange.

Four times a day for three years she had written nine marks in a book. Ten thousand marks, near enough. When a person does that, the marks stop being marks. They become a shape, and the shape has a texture, and you get so you can feel a wrong line the way a carpenter feels a warped plank: not by measuring it, but by putting your hand flat on it and going, hm.

That night, on the way back down the nineteen rungs, Sol thought about the tally and about the eleven years Roake had spent doing nothing, and she stopped on rung eleven with the wind coming up through the grating and the cloud below going silver with the first of the light.

She was still thinking about it when the ship's bell — the ordinary brass one by the wheelhouse, the one that had nothing to do with anything and was only for people — rang out four times for the change of watch, and the Meridian Gull went on across the Cloudsea at thirty knots and forty spans, on eight and a half bells, with no one aboard aware of it but two.

chapters.title: Chapter Three: A Bell That Rings Empty

blocks.c: Chapter Three: A Bell That Rings Empty
For five days nothing happened, which is the most dangerous thing that can happen.

Sol rang the third watch and the Ninth hummed full and true and beautiful. She wrote it in the tally. She began, in the sly way a mind protects itself, to construct explanations: a gust taking the tail; a trick of the cold; three years of the same nine notes finally curdling into imagination. She was sixteen. She was extremely willing to be told she was wrong about something, provided she got to sleep afterwards.
On the sixth day the Ninth rang empty in front of forty passengers.

It was the second watch, which is the sociable one — noon, sun on the cloud-tops, the observation gallery full of people from Antrell who had paid extra to watch the round the way you might pay to watch a man make glass. Dov Ilesca had the ropes off the lower frames for an inspection and was lying on his back under the number-four lift-frame with a spanner in his teeth. Roake was walking the line with her hands behind her back. Sol had the hammer.
Keel. Ladder. Kestrel. Quarrel. Mother. Lantern. Thimble. Widow.
A woman in a very good coat said, to a man in a worse one, "Is that all of them?"
"Nine," said the man, with the confidence of someone who has read one pamphlet. "There's nine."
Sol struck the Ninth.

The strike was perfect. She knew it in her wrist before she heard it: the flat of the hammer square on the sound-bow, the little jump of iron under the blow. The note went out across the gallery, high and bright, and the woman in the good coat made a small pleased noise.
And then the note ended, all at once, like a door closing on a room with a fire in it.

Forty passengers heard a bell ring. Forty passengers did not hear the thing they had not known they were listening for, which was the way the tail of the Ninth normally lay down over the top of Widow's tail and the two of them settled together like water finding a level. What they heard instead was a silence with an edge on it.

Nobody screamed. Passengers never scream at the actual dangerous thing; they scream at the second one. What they did was go quiet, the whole gallery, forty people all at once, because some part of the animal in each of them had felt the floor stop pushing up quite as hard as it had been.
The Gull dropped two spans.
It is worth explaining what two spans feels like, because the number is small and the feeling is not.

The deck goes soft. Everything that was standing on it becomes, for about a second and a half, a thing that is merely resting on it. A cup on a table lifts very slightly and comes back down without moving sideways. Your stomach, which has been quietly trusting the world all your life, notices that the world is negotiable.
Then the eight good bells take up the slack and the deck comes back and the whole thing is over, and everyone laughs, because that is the other thing passengers always do.

Roake did not laugh. Roake was moving before the drop finished, and she was not moving toward the Ninth. She was moving toward the gallery gate, where she took hold of the brass handle and swung it shut with a bang that made the woman in the good coat jump twice as high as the drop had.
"Gallery's closed," she said. "Weather."
"There isn't any weather," said the man with the pamphlet.
"There's always weather. That's the trouble with it."

They got the passengers out. Dov came out from under the lift-frame with grease to the elbow and an expression Sol had never seen on him, which was the expression of a person doing sums he did not like the shape of.
"Two spans," he said. "Off one bell."
"I know."

"No, you don't know, because you do sound and I do frames, so let me be insufferable for one minute." He wiped his hands on a rag that made them worse. "One bell in nine is about eleven parts in a hundred of the carry. Eleven parts of forty spans is four and a half. We dropped two. Which means either the Ninth was still giving us half, or something else took up half before the other bells did, and I don't know which of those frightens me more."
"The second one," said Sol.
"Yes," said Dov, unhappily. "The second one."

Roake came back down the line with the tally under her arm and her face like a closed shop. She put the ledger on the deck plating, knelt, and opened it, and Sol saw that she had not gone to fetch it from the cubby: she had been carrying it since before the round. She had brought the tally to the gallery.
She had known.
"Ferrant," said Roake. "Ring it again."
"You said never out of—"
"I said a bell struck alone has nothing to lean on. Ring the round. All nine. And Ilesca — put your hand flat on number-four frame and tell me when the carry comes back, to the second."

They rang it. Sol's arms had gone strange, that liquid feeling that comes after a fright, and she had to work at the four-beat count instead of letting it happen, but the eight rang full and Dov called the carry at each one, and then she walked to the stern and struck the Ninth.
It rang. It went quiet.
And Dov, with his hand flat on the frame and his eyes shut, said: "Late. Half a beat late. And it's — " He stopped. "That's not right. It's coming up."
"Coming up how?"

"Up. From below. The frame's taking it from underneath, not from the gallery." He opened his eyes and looked at the deck between his knees as though it had insulted his mother. "Sol, something rang under us."
Roake shut the tally.
"Right," she said. "Now it's in the book."

chapters.title: Chapter Four: The Tally Does Not Lie

blocks.c: Chapter Four: The Tally Does Not Lie

Captain Ovid Marn was a tall, tired, courteous man who had commanded the Meridian Gull for nine years and had never once, in Sol's hearing, raised his voice — a fact the crew found more alarming than shouting would have been.

He listened to all of it standing up, in the chart room, with his hands behind his back and the cloud going past the windows in long grey rolls. Roake told it. Sol confirmed it. Dov produced two pages of arithmetic which he had done in the eleven minutes since the round, and which Marn read carefully, all the way to the bottom, twice.
Then he said: "Bosun. Your recommendation."

"Ring five rounds a day instead of four until Antrell," said Roake. "Put a hand on the gallery through every watch. Sound the frames hourly. And I want the tally back to the start of the run laid out on that table."
"Granted, granted, granted, and how far back?"
"Eleven years."
Marn's eyebrows went up perhaps a quarter of an inch, which for him was a shout. "That is a great deal of ledger."
"Yes," said Roake.
"Why eleven?"
The bosun did not look at Sol. "Because that is when I first heard it and did nothing about it."
The tally, laid out, filled the chart table and then the floor.

They worked in shifts, because someone still had to run the ship: Sol, Dov, Roake, and — from the second evening, when it became apparent how much ledger there was — Purser Halloway, who was sixty, disapproved of everything, and turned out to be the fastest reader any of them had ever met.

The method was Dov's. For every round in eleven years, take the nine marks. Score them: full is nought, thin is one, dead is three. Add the nine. Write the sum in the margin of a fresh sheet, one line per round, four lines per day.
"You'll get a number that means nothing," said Halloway.
"I'll get a number that means nothing four times a day for four thousand days," said Dov, "and then I'll look at the shape of it, and the shape will mean something, because shapes always do."

It took eleven days to get through it. Sol did her watches, rang her rounds, slept in ninety-minute pieces, and read the handwriting of dead bell-hands until the columns swam. It was tedious in a way she had not known was available. It was also, she admitted to nobody, the happiest she had been aboard, because for the first time in three years she was not the only person acting as though the thing she had heard was real.
On the ninth day, Halloway found the first hole.
"This is not an error," the purser said, "and I want that understood, because I have found four thousand errors in this ledger and I know what an error looks like. This is not one."
He had eleven sheets in front of him. On each, a single line was ringed in his very small, very neat pencil.

"Twelve years ago, the Gull came into Antrell for her long refit. Two hundred and eleven days out of service. During a refit the bells are not rung, because the ship is on the cradles and there is nothing to hold up. The tally is closed. Look."
He turned a sheet. The lines stopped. A clerk's hand had written, on the last line: TALLY CLOSED — REFIT — REOPEN ON UNDOCK.

"And here is the reopening, two hundred and eleven days later. In a different hand, which is correct, because the bell-master changed during the refit. And here — " his pencil moved " — is the first round of the new run, and the Ninth is marked thin. And here is the second, thin. And the third, and the fourth. Thin, thin, thin, for nineteen days, and then it goes full and stays full for eleven years, and I would have called that a bell settling after a refit and thought no more about it."
"So would I," said Roake, quietly.

"Except." Halloway spread the eleven sheets. "Except that on each of these eleven days, spread across eleven years, the Ninth goes dead for exactly one round and then comes back. Not thin. Dead. One round, once, and back to full. Eleven times in eleven years, and here is the part I dislike: it is always the third watch, and it is always within a day of the ship passing the same point on the crossing."
Dov leaned over the sheets so fast he knocked a lamp. "Which point?"

Halloway put his pencil down on the chart, on a patch of the Cloudsea south of the shipping line, an unremarkable stretch of nothing that every ferry on the run went around rather than through, because the air there was dead and would not carry sound, and a ring-ship in dead air is a ship with a mouth full of wool.
The Quiet.
"There is nothing there," said Sol.
"There is nothing there," Halloway agreed, "on our charts."
Nobody said anything for a while. The Gull creaked and hummed and went on holding herself up.
Then Captain Marn, who had come in at some point and had been standing by the door long enough to hear most of it, said:
"Bosun, what is the name of the bell-master who signed the tally open after that refit?"

Roake did not need to look. Sol watched her not need to look, and understood that this was the moment the whole thing had been walking towards since a woman of fourteen heard a bell answer wrong and spent eleven years not saying so.
"Ysolde Kerrin," said Tamsin Roake. "She taught me. She signed my papers. And eleven years ago she went off this ship at Kettlemouth with a crate on a handcart, and nobody has seen her since."

chapters.title: Chapter Five: The Passenger Who Was Not on the Manifest

blocks.c: Chapter Five: The Passenger Who Was Not on the Manifest
The Meridian Gull carried four hundred and eleven passengers on that crossing, and Purser Halloway could name every one of them, which was not a boast but a job.

He named them for Sol on the fourteenth night, in the purser's office, going down the manifest with his pencil while she held the lamp, because she had asked him a question he found insulting and had then refused to withdraw it.
"You are asking me whether someone is aboard who should not be."
"Yes."
"On my ship."
"On our ship."

Halloway made the small dry sound that in another man would have been a laugh. "There are four hundred and eleven berths sold and four hundred and eleven bodies in them, and I counted twice, because I always count twice, because I am not a romantic." He turned the page. "However."
"However?"

"However, a berth is a thing you buy. It is not a thing you occupy. In cabin thirty-one there is a gentleman who bought two berths, boarded with no luggage, and has taken no meals in the saloon in fourteen days. The galley sends him a tray. He returns it empty, which tells me he eats, and clean, which tells me he washes the plate himself, and no man washes his own plate on a ferry he has paid double for unless he would rather not have a steward in his cabin."
Sol set the lamp down. "What's his name?"
"He gave the name Ivor Sallow." Halloway's pencil tapped the line. "It is a very good name. It is far too good. It is the sort of name a person chooses when they want a name that sounds like a name."
"Then he's not a passenger," said Sol.

"He is precisely a passenger. That is what makes him difficult. A stowaway I can put ashore; a passenger has bought the right to be a nuisance." Halloway closed the manifest with the flat finality of a man shutting a door on weather. "Do not go looking for him."
She went looking for him.
She found him three nights later on the ring gallery, at a quarter to four, standing at the rail by the Ninth with his hands in his coat pockets, watching her come up the nineteen rungs.
Sol had rehearsed this. What she had rehearsed was firm, and polite, and involved the phrase crew only.
What she said was: "You're standing under a bell."
"I am," the man agreed. "Is that dangerous?"
"It's rude."

That got a real laugh out of him, short and surprised. He was somewhere past fifty, with a face like a wall that had been repointed several times, and he wore a good coat badly, as though it had been bought for a different life. "Rude. Yes. That's fair. May I stay and be rude, or must I go?"
"You must go."

"Then let me be rude for one minute first, and I'll go and not come back." He took his hands out of his pockets and showed them to her, palms up, which is a thing people do when they want you to see that they are not holding anything, and which Sol had never once found reassuring. "You are the girl who hears the tail."
The wind came along the gallery and turned over the pages of the tally under her arm.
"Everyone hears the tail," she said.

"Everyone hears the strike. I have been on eleven crossings this year, on four ships, and I have stood under a great many bells at a great many hours, and I have watched a great many bell-hands write full in a book about a bell that was giving them nine parts in ten." He said it without malice, almost gently. "Do you know how many hands on this run can tell nine-tenths from ten-tenths? Three. You are one. Your bosun is one. The third is not on a ship any more."
"Who are you?"

"A man who buys and sells carry, which is a duller trade than it sounds and pays better than it should." He turned back to the rail and the dark. "Ring your round, Miss Ferrant. I'll listen from here and then I'll go below, and if you would like some advice from a person you have no reason to trust: when they hold the inquiry at Antrell — and they will hold an inquiry at Antrell — do not tell them what you heard. Tell them what is in the book."
"Why?"
"Because they can argue with you," he said, "and they cannot argue with eleven years of a dead woman's handwriting."
"She's not dead."

Sol had not known she was going to say it until it was out in the wind between them, and she watched the man in the good coat go absolutely still, the way a heron goes still, which is not the stillness of surprise but the stillness of a thing that has just seen a fish.

"No," he agreed, after a moment. "She isn't. Well done." He said it with real warmth, which somehow made it worse. "Do not put that in front of the commissioners either. They will want it to be a story about a wicked woman, because a wicked woman can be found and hanged and filed, and then everyone can go home. It is not a story about a wicked woman."
"What's it a story about?"
"Arithmetic," said Ivor Sallow, "which is the only kind of villain that has ever frightened me."

Sol rang the round. He listened, all nine, without moving. The Ninth hummed thin — not dead, thin — and she saw his chin come down a half-inch when it did, and knew that he had heard it too, and knew that he had wanted her to know.
When she looked round from writing in the tally he was gone, and the gallery gate was closed, and the ladder was empty all nineteen rungs down.
"Sallow," said Roake, when Sol told her. "Sallow, Sallow. That's not a name."
"That's what Halloway said."

"Halloway is right about names and wrong about everything else." The bosun was up to her elbows in the number-seven cradle, resetting a stay-bolt that had gone a quarter-turn loose in the drop. "Did he ask you for anything?"
"No."
"Did he offer you anything?"
Sol thought about it properly, because Roake asked questions the way a surgeon asks them, and a lazy answer wasted them.
"Advice," she said. "He told me to testify from the tally and not from my ears."
Roake stopped working.
"That," she said, "is very good advice, and I would like to know why a stranger is giving it to you two days before I was going to."

chapters.title: Chapter Six: Six Spans and Falling

blocks.c: Chapter Six: Six Spans and Falling
They lost the Ninth entirely at the turn of the fourth watch, eleven hours out from Antrell, in front of nobody at all.

It was Roake on the hammer — she had taken every round herself since the chart room, which meant she had slept four hours in three days and had reached the stage of tiredness where a person becomes very calm and slightly transparent. Sol had the frames with Dov. Halloway had the passengers, which meant he was in the saloon telling four hundred and eleven people a long and completely fictional anecdote about a customs officer, to keep their faces pointed away from the windows.
Keel. Ladder. Kestrel. Quarrel. Mother. Lantern. Thimble. Widow.
Sol had her palm flat on the number-four lift-frame, and she felt each one arrive: a shove, then a settling, then the long steady push of the carry taking hold. Eight shoves. Eight settlings.

Then Roake struck the Ninth and Sol's palm felt the frame go slack, and then — a half-beat later, from beneath the deck plating, from somewhere below the keel line, somewhere out in the cloud — she felt a pull.
Not a push. A pull. As if the ship were a rope and someone at the other end had taken up the slack.
"Down!" Dov shouted, from the far frame, and then the deck went out from under them.
Six spans in fourteen seconds.

That is not a fall. A ship of the Gull's tonnage cannot fall; there is too much carry laid in, and the eight bells were sound, and the frames held. What it is, is a settling — the ship finding a new height because the old one is no longer being paid for. It is exactly like the feeling of a chair being lowered under you by someone who is not looking at you while they do it.

Everything not tied down went to the deck. In the saloon, four hundred and eleven people discovered that Halloway's anecdote had a very long middle section. In the galley, a pot of soup for two hundred went across the floor in a single sheet and Cook Anselm said a word that later became a private joke among the stewards for eleven years. Sol went down on one knee hard enough to see white and got up again without noticing she had.

Roake was already ringing. Not the round — the round takes eleven minutes and they did not have eleven minutes. She was ringing the fall-off: Keel and Mother and Widow, the three deep bells, over and over, four beats, four beats, four beats, which is the oldest trick in the trade and which buys you height at the cost of tearing the tails of three bells to rags.
"Ballast!" the captain's voice, from the speaking tube, still courteous. "All of it. Now, please."

Dov went down the ladder without touching it, which Sol had heard about and never seen, and eleven seconds later the Gull began to shed water from her belly tanks in a grey rain that fell four hundred feet into cloud and was never seen again by anyone.
The ship came up two spans. Roake rang. The ship came up two more.

At six minutes past, with the deck level and the frames humming and the whole gallery smelling of scorched iron where a stay had gone dry, Bosun Roake stopped ringing, put the hammer down on the plating very carefully, as though it were sleeping, and sat down beside it.
"Ferrant," she said. "Tally."
Sol wrote it. Fourth watch. Roake. Keel full, Ladder full, Kestrel full, Quarrel full, Mother full, Lantern full, Thimble full, Widow full.
Ninth: dead.

And in the margin, because the margins were free, she wrote what her hand had felt on the frame, in five words that would be read aloud eleven days later in a room in Antrell by a man who intended them to sound ridiculous.
Something below took it. On purpose.

They came into Antrell the next evening on eight bells and prayer, at thirty-four spans and dropping half a span a watch, and the Company had a mooring gang and a fireboat and a very great many officials waiting at the tower, which is how the crew learned that news of the six-span settling had gone ahead of them by relay-flag.
Below decks it took two hours to put the ship back together, and Sol did it with everyone else, because on a ring-ship a bell-hand off watch is simply a pair of arms.

She carried buckets. She held a lamp for the carpenter while he chocked a bulkhead door that had sprung. She helped Cook Anselm scrape two hundred portions of soup off a galley floor, and Cook, who had been at sea in one form or another for thirty-one years, said the only useful thing anybody said that night, which was: "It's not the falling that gets people. It's that nobody tells them what happened after. Go and tell somebody what happened."

So Sol went into the saloon in her working leathers with soup on her boots and stood in front of four hundred and eleven frightened strangers, and told them that a bell had gone quiet, that eight had held, that ballast had been dropped, and that the ship was now at thirty-four spans, which was low, and safe, and ugly, and that the crew would be ringing five rounds a day instead of four all the way into Antrell so that the noise would be worse and the ship would be better.
Nobody applauded. A woman in a very good coat, who Sol recognised from the observation gallery, asked whether the bell could be fixed.
"Yes, ma'am," said Sol. "As soon as we know what's wrong with it."
It was, she reflected afterwards, the first entirely honest sentence anyone had spoken to those passengers since the drop, and it had taken a sixteen-year-old with soup on her boots to do it.

Sol stood at the rail as they warped in and watched the city come up: Antrell on its ridge, all pale stone and iron balconies, with the Foundry smoke going straight up in the still air of the evening, and the bell-towers on the four quarters ringing their own rounds for their own reasons.
Dov appeared beside her with his hands wrapped in gauze from the ballast valves.
"They're going to take the ship off the run," he said.
"They can't. It's the only run."

"That's why they can. If there was another ferry they'd have to compete with it. As it is they can put the Gull on the cradles for a season, sell the berths on the mail-packet at four times the price, and call it safety." He nodded down at the mooring gang. "See the man in grey by the bollard? That's Company Compliance. And the one behind him with the good coat and no luggage?"
Sol saw. Ivor Sallow, on the tower dock, in the middle of the officials, being greeted by name.
"He said he buys and sells carry," she said.
"Yes," said Dov. "I imagine that's true. It's usually the true thing that gets you."

chapters.title: Chapter Seven: The Inquiry at Antrell

blocks.c: Chapter Seven: The Inquiry at Antrell
The inquiry was held in a room with eleven windows, none of which opened, in the Company's offices on the Ridge, and it lasted two days and was not about what had happened.
It was about who could be blamed for it, which is a different subject and takes longer.

Sol had never been in a room like it. Panelling the colour of strong tea. A long table. Six commissioners of the Antrell Bell and Carry Company, of whom four never spoke at all, and a clerk in the corner who wrote everything down including, as far as Sol could tell, the coughs.

Captain Marn gave his account in ninety minutes, precisely, without notes, and the commissioners were gentle with him, because he was a captain of nine years' standing and because the loss of a captain is expensive.
They were not gentle with Roake.
"Bosun, you are the bell-master of the Meridian Gull."
"I am."
"For twenty-two years."
"Yes."
"In that time, the vessel has settled more than four spans on how many occasions?"
"Three."
"Three. And of those three, how many occurred in the last eleven days?"
"One," said Roake. "The other two were in eighty-nine, in the storm, when this Company's own weather office told four ships to run south of the Quiet and three of them came back."
The commissioner at the centre — a small, precise woman named Thole, who wore spectacles she did not need and used them the way a bird uses a wing — turned a page without hurry.
"Bosun, is your ninth bell sound?"
"Yes."
"You are certain."

"I have had my hand on that bell every day for twenty-two years. It is not cracked, it is not sprung, the crown is true and the sound-bow is even. There is nothing wrong with our bell." Roake leaned forward. "Something is taking its carry."
"Taking."
"Taking."
"Bosun," said Thole, "do you understand how that will read in a report?"
"I understand exactly how it will read in a report," said Roake, "and I have twenty-two years of tally on the table in front of you, and the tally does not read. The tally counts."
They called Sol on the second afternoon, and she nearly ruined everything in the first four minutes.
"You are the third-watch hand."
"Yes, ma'am."
"Sixteen years of age."
"Yes, ma'am."

"And it is your evidence that on the night of the fourteenth you heard the ninth bell ring and produce no hum, and that a hum then arrived late, and that you were able to determine, by ear, that this hum originated from outside the vessel."

Said in that room, in that voice, with the clerk's pen scratching, it sounded exactly as stupid as it was meant to sound. Sol felt her face go hot, and heard herself begin to say I know how it sounds, which is the sentence that loses every argument it is ever used in.
She stopped. She thought about a man in a bad good coat saying: they can argue with you, and they cannot argue with a dead woman's handwriting.
"No, ma'am," she said. "That's in the margin. My evidence is the book."
Thole's spectacles came down. "Explain."

"The tally has eleven years in it since the refit. Eleven times in those eleven years, the Ninth is marked dead for exactly one round and full again by the next. Every one of those eleven is the third watch. Every one of those eleven is within a day of the ship passing north of the Quiet. Eleven out of eleven, ma'am. Purser Halloway did the reading and Mister Ilesca did the arithmetic and both of them will tell you the odds of that being weather." She swallowed. "It's in the book. It's been in the book for eleven years. Nobody added it up because nobody had a reason to. We had a reason."
The clerk's pen had stopped.
"And the twelfth occasion," said Thole, "was six days ago, in daylight, in front of forty passengers."
"Yes, ma'am. Which is why we're here, and not still not-adding-it-up."
One of the four silent commissioners made a noise that might have been a cough.
Thole let the silence run for exactly as long as it was useful to her.
"The vessel's coal consumption," she said. "You have raised it in your written statement. Explain it, briefly, in words a shareholder would understand."
Sol had practised this one with Dov until she could do it asleep, which was fortunate, because she very nearly was.

"A ship that carries less is a ship that sits lower, ma'am. A ship that sits lower drags more. A ship that drags more burns more coal to keep her speed. The Gull has burned four parts in a hundred more coal every crossing for eleven years, and the Company has paid for every ton of it, and it's in your own accounts department two floors down." She stopped, and then added, because it was true and because she was too tired to be careful: "You've been buying that stolen carry back in coal for eleven years, ma'am. You just bought it in a different building."

The clerk in the corner wrote that down. Sol watched him write it and understood, too late, that a clerk writes down everything, including the sentences that will be read aloud later by people who wish you had never said them.
Thole took her spectacles off.
"Thank you, Miss Ferrant," she said. "That will do."
The finding, when it came, was a masterpiece of not saying anything.

The Meridian Gull was found to have suffered a carry deficiency of undetermined cause. Bosun Roake was neither censured nor cleared, which in Company language means censured. The vessel was permitted to continue on the run for a probationary period of forty days, with an additional round per watch and a Company observer aboard at all times.
The Company observer, said the letter, would be Mr. Ivor Sallow.
Sol found him afterwards on the tower dock, in the smoke and the evening, watching the gangs load coal into a mail-packet.
"You knew what the finding would be before you gave me the advice," she said.

"I wrote most of it," said Sallow. "That's what an observer does; he observes early." He glanced sideways at her. "You did well in there. You did better than well. You made a room full of men who are paid not to be curious spend four minutes being curious."
"They gave us forty days."

"They gave you forty days on a run that takes eleven, which is three crossings and a little. Three crossings to find out what is taking your bell's voice." He put on his hat. "I would start with where it was made. Everything about a bell is decided in the four seconds the metal goes into the mould, and the Foundry keeps a book too. Foundries always keep a book. It is the only trade worse than yours for writing things down."

chapters.title: Chapter Eight: What the Foundry Poured

blocks.c: Chapter Eight: What the Foundry Poured

The Antrell Foundry stood on the north face of the ridge with its back to the wind and its front open to a yard full of broken things, and it had been casting bells for the ferry line for a hundred and forty years.

Sol and Dov went up on their one clear morning, with Roake's grudging permission and Halloway's much more useful letter of introduction, and were kept waiting in a shed for an hour and a half by a girl of about twelve who was clearly enjoying it.
"Master Ottring will see you when the pour's off."
"When's the pour off?"
"When it's off."

The pour came off at eleven. They knew because the whole hill went quiet in a way that made the hair stand up on Sol's arms; the roar of the furnace stopped, and into the silence came a long, low, absolutely enormous hum, as the metal in the mould began to cool and to argue with itself about what shape it was going to be.
"That's not a bell yet," said Dov.
"No," said Sol, listening with her whole spine. "But it's deciding."

Master Ottring was eighty if she was a day, four feet and eleven inches of leather apron and opinion, and she read Halloway's letter twice and then looked at the two of them for an uncomfortably long time.
"Gull's ninth," she said at last. "You want the pour book for the Gull's ninth."
"Yes, ma'am."
"Why?"
Dov opened his mouth to be diplomatic. Sol got there first.
"Because it rings and something else hums," she said, "and I want to know what else came out of that mould."
The old woman's face did something complicated.
"Come on, then," she said. "Mind the floor. It's hot in patches and it doesn't tell you which."

The pour book was chained to a lectern, which Sol thought excessive until Ottring explained that a foundry's pour book is the only document in the world that can prove a bell is what it claims to be, and that people had been murdered over less.

Bells are not simply cast. They are cast from a specific melt, and the melt has a character — the tin high or low, the copper from this mine or that, the hour of the day, the temper of the metal-master's stomach — and two bells cast from the same melt on the same day are called a pair, and a pair is a problem.

"Sympathy," said Ottring, turning pages with a hooked finger. "Strike one, the other answers. Any two bells will do it a little; it's only metal talking to metal. A true pair will do it across a valley. A true pair, tuned the same and hung the same, will do it across a great deal more than a valley, and that is why this Foundry has not poured a true pair in ninety years, and why the law says you may not, and why the law is the least of the reasons."
"What's the biggest reason?" said Dov.

"The carry goes to whichever is rung truer." Ottring did not look up. "Two bells, one voice, and the voice sits with whoever plays it better. That is not a superstition, young man, that is a fact you can weigh on a scale, and the last people to find it out the hard way put a town in a lake."
"Show us," said Sol.
Ottring looked up. "Show you what?"
"Sympathy. You said any two bells do it a little. Show us a little."

The old woman put her hooked finger in the page to keep the place, which is a thing Sol's mother had done and which nearly undid her on the spot, and led them out into the yard where the seconds hung: four small bells on a rack, rejects and test pours, the sort of iron that never makes it onto a ship.

"That one and that one came off the same melt in Ninthmonth," said Ottring. "Not a true pair — I'd have broken them up. Cousins. Put your hand on the second one. Flat. Don't grip it, you're not strangling it."
Sol laid her palm on the cold rim.
Ottring struck the first bell with a wooden mallet, four feet away, and Sol felt the bell under her hand wake up.

It was not loud. It was not, in any ordinary sense, a sound at all. It was a small persistent trembling in the metal beneath her palm, like the pulse in a wrist, and it went on for the whole length of the other bell's tail and then stopped when the tail stopped, and Sol stood in a foundry yard in Antrell with her hand on a rejected bell and thought about a ship dropping six spans in fourteen seconds.
"That's cousins," she said. "Four feet apart."

"That's cousins," Ottring agreed. "A true pair would do that with a mountain in between, and it wouldn't stop when the tail stopped, because it isn't listening to the sound. It's listening to the metal remembering the same afternoon."
She went back inside.
She stopped turning.

"Here," she said. "Gull's ninth. Poured the eleventh of Fourthmonth, year forty-one, from melt sixty-two. Tuned by Ottring — that's my mother — and hung by the Bellwrights' Company in the spring." Her finger moved down the page and stopped. "And melt sixty-two ran two moulds."
The shed was extremely quiet.
"Two," said Sol.

"Two. Big melt. They cast the Gull's ninth and they cast a second casting off the same metal, and here is the entry for it, in my mother's hand, and here is what it says." Ottring turned the book around so they could both see. "Delivered — Kettlemouth, wharfside, to the account of the Lowspire Platform Company. And under it, in a different ink, twelve years later, somebody has written: RETURNED, UNSOLD, HELD."
"Held where?" said Dov.

Ottring looked at them both, and Sol understood that the old woman had known the answer to this question since the moment they walked in, and had wanted to make them earn it, because that is how you make a person believe an unbelievable thing.

"Held aboard the Meridian Gull," she said. "In her forward hold, for eleven years, until a bell-master by the name of Kerrin signed it out at Kettlemouth on a handcart, on a wet Tuesday, with nobody's permission but her own."

chapters.title: Chapter Nine: Dov's Arithmetic

blocks.c: Chapter Nine: Dov's Arithmetic
Dov Ilesca did his best thinking upside down, which was inconvenient for everyone.

Sol found him that night in the frame-space under the gallery, hanging by his knees from a cross-member with a slate on his chest and chalk dust in his eyebrows, in the manner of a bat that had taken up accountancy.
"The blood goes to your head," she said.
"That's the idea. Hold the lamp. Higher. There." He wrote something, rubbed it out, wrote it again. "Right. I know how much they're taking."
Sol sat down on a bracket. "Go on."

"Eleven parts in a hundred is one bell in nine, agreed? That's if a bell goes fully dead and nothing else changes. But when the Ninth went dead on us we lost two spans, then six. Two is less than eleven parts of forty. Six is more. That bothered me for eleven days and now it doesn't, and the reason it doesn't is that I was doing the sum for a bell that had stopped, and the bell hasn't stopped. It's ringing. Somebody else is spending it."
"Spending."

"Carry isn't a thing the bell makes. Everyone says that and everyone is wrong, including me until Tuesday. The bell doesn't make carry, the bell holds a note, and the note is a claim on the air. If two bells hold the same note, the air has to decide which claim it honours, and it honours the one that's rung truer, and truer is a technical word and I have spent three days finding out that it means: rung closer to the interval." He tapped the slate. "Four beats. We ring four beats between strikes because that's the tradition. The tradition is wrong. Or rather it's rounded. The true interval on a melt-sixty-two bell is four beats and about a tenth."
Sol's stomach did something unpleasant. "You're saying they're ringing better than us."

"I'm saying they're ringing exactly, and we're ringing approximately, and they've had eleven years to practise." He unhooked his knees and came down in a controlled fall that Sol had learned not to react to. "Here's the shape of it. Look."
He held the slate to the lamp.

items: Eleven times in eleven years the Ninth went fully dead for one round. Those are the days they rang a full sequence — took everything.

Every other day of those eleven years, our tally says the Ninth hummed full, and it did hum full, to any ear on this ship except one. But the carry has been down by about a part in a hundred the whole time, which shows up nowhere except in coal.

Coal. The Gull has burned four per cent more coal per crossing since the refit, every crossing, for eleven years, because a ship carrying less carry sits lower and drags more. Halloway has the coal ledgers. Nobody ever put the coal ledger next to the tally because they live in different offices.
One part in a hundred, taken continuously, for eleven years, is an enormous amount of carry, and it did not go into the air. It went into holding something up.

blocks.c: "How big a something?" said Sol.
Dov wiped the slate with his sleeve and drew a rectangle.

"That's the Gull. Forty spans of carry, eight hundred tons, four hundred and eleven passengers and change." He drew a second rectangle beside it, a third the size. "That's what one part in a hundred, banked for eleven years and topped up eleven times, will hold at low altitude in still air, and I have checked it twice and I do not want to have checked it right."
Sol looked at the little chalk box.
"That's not a bell in a shed," she said.
"No."
"That's a town."

They took it to Halloway, because everything went to Halloway now, and the purser listened to the whole of it with his hands folded and then did the single most frightening thing Sol saw anybody do that month, which was to get out the coal ledgers without being asked.
"You wish to know," he said, "whether the four per cent is real."
"Yes."

"It is real. I have known it was real for nine years and I have written four memoranda about it, and each of those memoranda came back from the Ridge with a note saying that fuel efficiency on the Antrell run had declined in line with fleet averages." He pulled a bound quarto out of the case. "Which is true. It has. Because every ship on this run passes north of the Quiet."
Dov stopped with his chalk halfway to the slate.
"Every ship."

"Four ships. The Gull, the Cormorant, the Sabine Rey and the mail-packet." Halloway licked his thumb and turned pages. "Fleet average went up four per cent in the year after the Gull's refit and has stayed there. Everybody assumed it was the price of coal, or the age of the frames, or the weather, because when everybody's number moves at once nobody looks for a thief. They look for a season."
"But it's only us," said Sol. "It's only our bell that's paired."
"It is only your bell that is paired," Halloway agreed. "So either the fleet average moved for a different reason at exactly the same time — "
" — or she's taking it off all four," said Dov, in a small voice, "and only ours has a twin, so only ours shows in the tally."
The purser closed the ledger.

"I have been a clerk for forty-one years," he said. "I will tell you the worst thing I know about numbers, which is this: a figure that has been wrong for a long time stops being an error and becomes a baseline, and then it is defended. Four per cent has been in the Company's budget for eleven years. It is in the fares. It is in my own salary. If we prove where it went, we do not merely embarrass a commission. We take four per cent away from eleven people who have grown used to it."

chapters.title: Chapter Ten: The Hold Below the Hold

blocks.c: Chapter Ten: The Hold Below the Hold
Ships have layers, and the layers have layers, and a ring-ship's forward hold is where the layers stop being architecture and start being archaeology.

They went down at the turn of the first watch: Sol with a lamp, Dov with a pry-bar, and Roake with the plan of the ship rolled under her arm and an expression that dared anyone to ask what she was doing awake for the fourth night running.

The forward hold ran from the collision bulkhead to the ballast trunk, forty feet of iron ribs and stacked crates and the smell of cold rope. Mail sacks in nets. A crated spare frame from the eighty-nine refit that nobody had ever unpacked because unpacking it would mean admitting they might need it. Three centuries of the sort of objects that get put down somewhere for a moment.
Roake unrolled the plan against a rib and held her lamp to it.
"There," she said. "Between frames nine and eleven. On the plan it's a void."
"It's not a void," said Dov, who had gone ahead. "There's a wall."

The wall was iron, painted the same grey as everything else, riveted at top and bottom, and it had been there long enough for the paint to have the same eleven layers as its neighbours. Sol would have walked past it a hundred times. She had walked past it a hundred times.
Sol put her hand on it. Then she put her ear on it, which is a thing you learn to do in the trade before you learn almost anything else, because iron carries and air lies.
"It's hollow," she said. "It's hollow and it's dry. Everything on this deck sweats. This doesn't."
"Because it's been sealed," said Roake. "Sealed things don't breathe. Ilesca?"
"There's no hatch."
"There is always a hatch. Nobody riveted a wall in place around a thing they intended to take out again. Find it."
It took Dov nineteen minutes to find the four dogs disguised as rivet heads, and when they came off the panel swung out on hinges that had been greased within the last decade.
Inside was a space the size of a large wardrobe, and it was empty, and it had not always been.
Sol put the lamp in and the three of them looked in silence at what eleven years of absence looks like.

There was a cradle bolted to the deck: a bell cradle, a good one, sized for something about the height of a kneeling person. There were rope marks worn deep into the timber of the cradle's yoke, and in the marks, a fine grey powder that Roake touched and smelled and said was tallow and iron. There were four chocks to stop a heavy thing shifting in a sea-way, and one of the chocks had been split and repaired with a plate, and the plate had been fitted by someone who knew what they were doing.
And on the inside of the door, in chalk that had survived eleven years because nothing in that space ever moved, there was a list.
Sol held the lamp up to it.
One. Four and one. Two. Four and one. Three. Four and one. Four. Four and one. Five. Four and one. Six. Four and one. Seven. Four and one. Eight. Four and one. NINE — hold — count nine — strike.
"That's a round," said Dov.
"That's our round," said Sol. Her voice had gone strange in her own ears. "Four and one. Four beats and one tenth. She wrote the true interval on the inside of a door eleven years ago."

Roake had not spoken since the panel came off. She stood with her lamp held low, looking at the chalk in a hand she plainly recognised, and after a while she reached out and put two fingers against the wood beside it, not touching the letters, the way you touch the frame of a picture.

"She practised in here," Roake said. "Every night for eleven years, while I was up on the gallery ringing four flat, she was down here in the dark with her own bell and her own count, getting it right."
"Bosun—"

"I heard it at fourteen." Roake's voice was perfectly level, which was how Sol knew. "I heard the Ninth answer wrong and I told my bell-master, who was Ysolde Kerrin, and she said: good ear, girl, don't waste it on ghosts. And I believed her, because she was the best hand I ever saw and because I wanted her to be pleased with me." She lowered the lamp. "She was standing three feet from a wall with a bell behind it."
Sol did not know what to do with any of that, so she did what she always did, which was to work.

She measured the cradle. She measured the yoke and the depth of the rope marks and the height of the chocks, and she wrote the numbers on the back of her hand because she had no paper, and when she had all of them she stood in the doorway of a wardrobe-sized room in the bow of a sky-ferry and built the bell in her head out of the shape of the hole it had left.

Eleven hundred pounds, near enough. Thirty-one inches at the mouth. Hung with a straight yoke rather than a canted one, which meant a hand ringing it stood square to it and used both arms, which meant it had been meant to be rung by somebody strong, or somebody stubborn, for a very long time.
"Bosun," she said. "It's the same size as ours."
"I know."

"No — I mean it's exactly the same size as ours. It's not a spare. Nobody casts a spare to the same tuning; a spare's cast a hair sharp so you can take metal off it and match whatever it's replacing." Sol looked at the rope marks. "This was cast to be rung alongside. From the beginning. Somebody meant there to be two, forty-one years ago, and then it sat in a cupboard for thirty."
Dov, crouched by the chocks with his lamp, said, "Then the crime isn't eleven years old."
"No," said Roake. "The crime is that somebody put it in a cupboard."

Nobody slept. At the turn of the second watch Sol rang the round — four beats and one tenth, an interval her arms did not know and her ear did — and every bell hummed full, and the Ninth hummed fuller than she had heard it in three years, and the Gull came up half a span all by herself.
Dov, hand flat on the frame, laughed out loud, once, like a bark.
"Ferrant," he said, "you just took some of it back."

chapters.title: Chapter Eleven: Kettlemouth in the Rain

blocks.c: Chapter Eleven: Kettlemouth in the Rain
The Gull came into Kettlemouth in weather that had been going on so long it had stopped being weather and become a climate.

Sol had grown up in that rain. It comes off the Cloudsea in sheets and hits the harbour wall and goes upward, so that in Kettlemouth it rains from below, and every native of the town walks with their collar up and their hat brim down and their face set in the particular expression of a person being insulted continuously by the sky.
She had eight hours ashore. She spent one of them at her mother's grave, which took four minutes and then twenty-six minutes of standing there not thinking of anything.

The yard where her mother had walked rope was still there, four streets back from the wall, and Sol went past it out of habit and stood at the gate for a while. Ropewalking is the oldest boring job in the world: you go backwards down a long shed paying out fibre while the strands turn, and you do it for eleven hours, and at the end of it there is a rope. Her mother had been able to feel a fault in a lay through the ball of her thumb, and had once stopped a whole walk over four inches of bad hemp, and had been extremely unpopular for it for about a week and then correct for the following thirty years, since the rope in question was for a mooring gang.

Sol had not thought about that in three years. She thought about it now, at the gate, in the rain that came upward, and understood with a lurch that she had spent a month doing precisely what her mother had done: putting her hand on a long thing and saying, there is a fault in here, and being disliked for it.
Then she went to find Halloway in the harbour registry, because a purser ashore in his home port is a weapon.

"Kerrin, Ysolde," said the registry clerk. "There'll be a discharge. There's always a discharge." He went away and came back with a card. "There you are. Discharged at own request from the Meridian Gull, wharfside, eleven years back. Cargo declared: one bell, personal property, duty paid in full." He turned the card over. "And an onward carriage note. Wharf to the Low Stair."
Halloway's pencil stopped.
"The Low Stair is not a place you take a bell," he said.

"The Low Stair isn't a place you take anything," the clerk agreed, cheerfully. "It's a hole in the cliff with a lift at the bottom of it that hasn't been licensed since I was a boy. It goes down below the cloudline. There used to be a mining platform down there — coal and cinder-iron, before the seams gave out."
"Lowspire," said Sol.
"That's the one. Company shut it in seventy-eight. Cut it loose, they said. Everybody came up."
"Did they?" said Halloway.

The clerk opened his mouth, and stopped, and looked at the card in his hand with the expression of a careful man who has just heard the first four notes of a tune he has been trying not to hum for thirty years.
"Well," he said, "that's what the notice said."
They walked back along the harbour wall in the sideways rain, and Halloway talked, which was rare, and Sol listened, which was not.

"I was a clerk in this town in seventy-eight," he said. "The platform was five hundred souls when it was working and about two hundred at the end. Miners, their families, a school, a chandler, two chapels who hated each other. When the seams gave out, the Company put up a notice saying the platform would be cut loose at midsummer and offering passage up for anyone with a ticket."
"With a ticket."

"With a ticket." He put his collar up. "A ticket was eleven shillings. A miner at the end of a dead seam has no shillings, he has credit at a Company store that is about to stop existing. And it is a very long way down, Miss Ferrant, and the platform hangs on a frame that hangs on carry, and when the Company pulls the bells off a platform, the platform does not fall in a day. It falls in a season. Slowly. Which means everyone has time to watch it happen."
Sol thought about the little chalk box on Dov's slate.
"How many stayed?" she said.

"The Company's number is nil. The Company's number is always nil." Halloway shrugged. "The chandler's daughter came up in eighty-one with a baby and no ticket and could not say how, and there was a certain amount of trouble about it, and then the file was closed."
They walked. Below them the harbour water was the colour of a nail.

"Eleven years ago," Sol said, "a bell-master with the best ear on the run signed out a bell that made a pair with ours, and took it down a lift nobody licenses, to a platform with two hundred people on it that the Company says is empty."
"Yes."
"And she's been stealing carry off a ferry ever since."
"Yes."
"Halloway. Is she the villain of this?"
The purser was quiet for eleven paces.
"That," he said, "is the correct question, and I would be extremely careful about who else you ask it in front of."

The Low Stair was where the clerk had said it was: a stone arch in the cliff below the fish market, with a gate across it, and on the gate a notice board with four notices on it, three of them illegible with age and the fourth quite new.
Sol read the new one twice.

It was a Company bill, printed that spring, offering a reward of eleven guineas for information concerning the unlicensed operation of the lift beyond the arch, and it had been up long enough to go soft at the corners, and somebody had written across the bottom of it, in pencil, in a hand that had pressed hard enough to tear the paper:
They know. They have always known. They only mind when it is written down.
"That's not Kerrin's hand," said Halloway.

"No," said Sol. She put her fingers against the gate. It was cold and slick and the hinges had been greased, recently, by somebody who wanted a gate that opened quietly. "It's somebody's, though. Halloway — eleven guineas is nine weeks of a stevedore's pay, and that bill has been up since spring, and nobody in this town has claimed it."
The purser looked at the gate for a long moment.

"No," he agreed. "Kettlemouth is not a sentimental place. But it is a harbour town, and every family in it has somebody who went down a hole for money once." He turned his collar up again. "Come along. We have four hours and I want to see the lift's power bill, which will be in the gas company's ledger, because a lift that does not exist still cannot run on nothing."

chapters.title: Chapter Twelve: What Roake Owed

blocks.c: Chapter Twelve: What Roake Owed
Sallow came aboard for the outward crossing with a folding desk, four crates of Company forms, and the manner of a man moving into a house he intends to be buried in.

He set up in the chart room. He asked for the tally. Marn gave it to him, because a captain under probation gives an observer whatever he asks for, and because Marn had understood something about Sallow that took Sol another two days: the man had not asked to see the coal ledgers, and he should have, and the only reason not to ask for a document is that you already know what is in it.
"He's not here to catch us," Sol said, on the gallery, at four in the morning, with the rain gone and the stars enormous.
"No," said Roake. "He's here to be a witness. There's a difference and the difference is who he intends to give evidence against."
"The Company?"

"Ferrant, in my experience there is no such thing as the Company. There's eleven people who between them own a run, and about four hundred who work for them and say we when they mean they." Roake ran her thumb along the sound-bow of the Ninth, checking for the tenth of an inch of grit that would flatten a tail. "The question I want answered is what Sallow gets. Nobody rides eleven crossings a year to buy and sell nothing."
He got his answer three days out, and he got it from Marn, who had gone about it in the direct way that captains can.

"I asked him," Marn told them in the chart room, "what his interest was. He said: a lease. I said, on what. He said, on a mineral seam that a certain company wrote off as exhausted in seventy-eight on the strength of a survey conducted by a man they were paying to say so. I said, that is a serious allegation. He said, it is not an allegation, it is an opportunity, and I have been four years assembling it, and I would rather assemble it in the company of a ship's officer than alone."
"He wants the seam," said Roake.

"He wants the seam. And to get the seam he needs the platform to exist legally, and for the platform to exist legally he needs it not to be a criminal enterprise, and for it not to be a criminal enterprise he needs a bell licence, and for a bell licence he needs — " Marn spread his hands.
"Us," said Sol.

"A bell-master of standing, an ear nobody can impeach, an engineer who can show his working and a purser with forty-one years of unblemished ledgers." The captain sat down, which he did about twice a year. "We are not being investigated, Bosun. We are being recruited."

Sol rang the round at four and one. The bells came up full and the Ninth hummed like a struck wire, and she wrote it in the tally in the column and, in the margin, the interval, because someone eleven years from now was going to need to know what they had changed and when.
When she looked up, Roake was sitting on the number-eight cradle with her hands hanging between her knees, and she looked, for the first time in three years, like an old woman.
"Sit down," she said. "I owe you a thing."
"Bosun—"

"Sit down, and don't be kind about it, I've had enough kindness this month to last me out." Roake waited until Sol sat. "You want to know why I stopped asking questions at fourteen. It wasn't because Kerrin told me not to waste my ear on ghosts. It was what she said after."
The wind moved along the gallery and set the loose end of a lanyard tapping.

"She said: Tamsin, some people hear it and some don't, and the ones who do get given a choice sooner or later, and the choice is always the same. It is always: hold this up, or hold that up. And she said: whichever one you pick you'll spend the rest of your life being told you picked wrong by people who have never held anything up in their lives." Roake looked at her hands. "I was fourteen. It sounded like the wisest thing I had ever heard. It sounded like being let off."
"It sounds like an excuse," said Sol, and then went cold, because you do not say that to a bosun.
Roake laughed. It was not a happy sound but it was a real one.

"It is an excuse," she said. "It's a very good one. That's what makes it dangerous, and that's what she is: she's the best hand who ever rang on this run and she has an excellent excuse, and there are two hundred people alive underneath the cloudline who are alive because of it."
Sol stared at her. "You know."
"I have known for eleven days, same as you."
"No. Bosun — you knew before. You knew when Halloway found the eleven dates. You said eleven years to the captain before anyone had put a single line together."
Tamsin Roake looked out at the cloud going silver in the east.

"I said eleven years," she said, "because eleven years ago I stood on the wharf at Kettlemouth in the rain and watched my bell-master push a handcart with a bell on it towards the Low Stair, and she saw me see her, and she nodded to me, and I nodded back."
"Bosun."
"And then I went and rang the second watch," said Roake, "four beats flat, like a fool, for eleven years."

Sol did not say anything for a while, because there was nothing to say that was not either cruel or useless, and she was learning, slowly, that those are usually the only two things available and that the correct move is to say neither.
At last she said: "Why tell me now?"

"Because in about four weeks somebody is going to have to decide what we do about two hundred people who are alive on stolen carry, and it will not be the captain and it will not be the Company." Roake stood up, and her knees made the noise they always made. "It will be whoever is holding the hammer. And I am fifty-nine and I have already made my decision once, and I made it badly, and I do not entirely trust myself not to make it the same way twice."
"So it's mine."
"It is going to be yours whether either of us likes it," said the bosun. "I would simply prefer that you had eleven years less than I did to think about it."
She went to the ladder, and stopped, and turned round.

"Ferrant. What I said in the cubby, the first night. Do better than that. I meant it kindly and it came out like a threat, and I have been thinking about it for a month." She looked at the row of iron hearts in the dark. "You have already done better than that. Whatever happens next, you did the part I couldn't, and you did it in eleven days, at sixteen, with everybody telling you not to. Write that in the margin somewhere."

chapters.title: Chapter Thirteen: The Quiet

blocks.c: Chapter Thirteen: The Quiet

The Quiet is a patch of the Cloudsea about eleven miles across, south of the shipping line, and every chart made in the last hundred years draws it as a plain grey oval with no soundings and the single word AVOID.
It is not a storm. Nothing happens in it. That is the entire problem.

"Dead air," said Marn, in the chart room, with the whole of the ship's officers around the table and Sallow at the end of it taking notes he did not need. "Air that will not carry sound. We do not know why. The weather office has four theories, of which two are religious. What we know is that a bell rung in the Quiet is a bell rung in a pillow: the strike is there, the tail is not, and a ring-ship in dead air has about ninety minutes of carry in hand and then begins to go down."
"And the eleven dates," said Roake, "are every one of them the day we pass north of it."
"Yes."
"Which means she rings when we are nearest, and it means the thing she is ringing to is somewhere inside it."
"That," said Marn, "is my reading also, and I dislike it, because I cannot take four hundred and eleven passengers into dead air on a theory."
Sallow's pen stopped. Everyone looked at him, which he had arranged.
"You cannot," he agreed. "But the Meridian Gull carries a tender."

The tender was called the Sprat and she was thirty-one feet of patched grey canvas over a light iron frame, with a single bell no bigger than a bucket, and she hung off the Gull's port quarter on davits, and her entire purpose in life was to take four people and the mail to places the ferry could not moor.
Sol had been aboard her twice. Both times she had been sick.

"Four of us," said Marn. "No more, and I want that understood. Bosun Roake, because she is bell-master and because I cannot stop her. Mister Ilesca, for the frames. Mister Sallow, who represents the Company and who has, I notice, volunteered with suspicious speed."
"I want to see it," said Sallow, mildly. "I have spent nineteen years buying and selling a thing I have never once been able to look at. Allow an old clerk his day out."
"And the fourth," said Marn, and stopped, and Sol watched a captain of nine years' standing decide something he did not want to decide.
"Sir," she said. "You need an ear."
"You are sixteen."
"Yes, sir. I'm also the only person on this ship who can tell you, from the sound, whether we're getting closer to it."
Marn looked at her for a long moment.
"Ferrant," he said, "if I come back from this run without you, I will be asked by a great many people why I permitted it, and I will not have a good answer."
"No, sir," said Sol. "But if you come back from this run without knowing what's under us, you'll be asked the same question by the next captain of this ship, and he won't have one either."
Roake, behind her, made a small noise of appalled satisfaction, like a woman watching her dog fetch a stick from a river she had specifically told it to avoid.

"Very well," said Marn. "Four. And Bosun — the ship rings four beats and one tenth in your absence, and I want that written into the standing orders in your hand before you leave, because if this goes badly I intend the Gull to keep the one useful thing to come out of it."

Roake wrote it. It took her four lines and it changed a trade that had not changed in four hundred years, and afterwards Sol thought that this was the most Roake thing that had ever happened: the woman had climbed into a boat expecting not to come back, and had spent her last eleven minutes aboard correcting a procedure.
They dropped the Sprat at the third watch, in the dark, four miles north of the Quiet, with the Gull's lamps blazing above them and getting smaller.

It is a bad feeling to go down. Everything in a ring-ship's life is arranged around not going down; the entire trade, the tally, the ledgers, the four hundred years of ritual, all of it exists to keep a boat above a line, and to point a nose deliberately below that line feels like putting your hand in a fire to see whether the stories are true.
Sol sat in the bow with her hands on the rail and her ear turned outward.

The Sprat's little bell rang every two minutes on a clockwork trip, which was the only concession the trade had ever made to devices, and each ring came back off the cloud with a tail like a piece of wool being drawn through a knot-hole: thin, but there.
At eleven minutes past, the tail shortened.
"Slow," she said.
At fourteen minutes, it halved.
"Slower."

At sixteen minutes past, the little bell rang and Sol heard the strike and then nothing at all, not a hum, not a tail, not the small returning breath that sound makes off cloud, and the silence came down over the boat like a hand over a mouth.
Dov swore quietly and comprehensively.
"Bosun," said Sol, "we're in it."
Roake's voice, from the stern, sounded like it was coming through a wall, although she was eleven feet away.
"Then listen," she said, "for the one thing that shouldn't be here."

They listened. The engine was a series of muffled thumps. The wind had stopped making any noise whatever, which was the worst part. Sol shut her eyes and did the thing she had done four times a day for three years, which was to stop listening for a sound and start listening for the space a sound leaves.
And in the dead air of the Quiet, from below and to port, she felt a hum come up through the boat's frame and into the bones of her feet.
Four beats and one tenth. Nine of them. Then a hold, a count of nine, and a strike.
"Down and left," she said, and her voice shook, and she did not care. "It's right underneath us and it's ringing right now."

Roake put the tiller over. Dov, who had spent the descent holding a lantern and being professionally sceptical, put his hand flat on the Sprat's frame and said nothing at all for eleven seconds, which for Dov was a sworn affidavit.
"She's right," he said. "It's under us."
"How far?"
"I do not have an instrument for that. I have a boy's hand on a piece of iron."
"Then guess."
"Four hundred feet," said Sol, before Dov could. "Give or take. It's the shape of the arrival. Close things come up hard and stop; far things come up soft and keep coming."

Sallow, in the bow, with his hat off and his hair standing straight up in the dead air, said, to nobody in particular: "Nineteen years. Nineteen years I have bought and sold this and I have never once heard it, and a child hears it through the bottom of a boat."
"You can't hear it," said Sol. "Nobody can hear it. You feel it."
"Then what is your ear for?"
"Knowing what to feel for," said Sol, and put her palms flat on the rail, and took them down.

chapters.title: Chapter Fourteen: Lowspire

blocks.c: Chapter Fourteen: Lowspire
They came out of the cloud at four hundred feet and there it was.
Sol's first thought, which she was ashamed of for years afterwards, was that it was smaller than it should have been.

Lowspire hung in the clear air under the cloudline: a platform of black iron and grey timber, eleven-sided, perhaps four hundred feet across, with a shanty town grown over it like moss on a stone. Chimneys. Washing lines strung between chimneys, in the still air, holding actual washing. A dozen roofs of tarred canvas and a dozen more of slate that had plainly been carried down one sheet at a time. The old winding gear of the mine stood at one end, stripped to its ribs.
And in the middle, on a stone plinth that was the only stone in the whole structure, under a shingle roof on four posts: a bell.
It was the size of a kneeling person. Even from a quarter-mile Sol knew the shape of it, the way you know a relative's walk at a distance. She had rung its twin four times a day for three years.
