Below the platform, in the dark, the iron went down and down in a lattice into the cinder-cliff, and the whole thing was very obviously not sitting on anything.
"It's hanging," said Dov, in the voice of a man watching his own arithmetic breathe. "Look at the frame. Look at the sag on the north side. That is a structure being held up, right now, by a note."
"By our note," said Sallow.
"By a note," said Roake.

The Sprat put down on a landing stage that had been built for boats twice her size and maintained by people with more will than materials. Sol saw the repairs first: a stringer spliced with a mine rail. A stanchion made from a chapel gate. A whole section of decking laid in mismatched planks, sanded, oiled, and kept better than the Gull's own.
Then she saw the people.

There were perhaps sixty of them on the stage and coming down the ways towards it, and they were not what she had braced for. She had braced for something out of a broadsheet: hollow faces, rags, the picturesque misery that towns tell each other about. What she got was sixty people in patched but mended clothes, most of them staring at the Sprat with the exact expression of a household hearing an unexpected knock at eleven at night.
A man at the front had a lamp and no weapon and was so frightened that his hand shook the light.
"You're not the mail," he said.
"No," said Sallow, stepping onto the stage as though he did this every day. "Though I notice that you expect mail, which is interesting, and which I shall be putting in my report."
"Sallow," said Roake.
"Bosun."

"Shut up." Roake stepped past him, took her hat off, and said, to the man with the lamp, in a voice Sol had never heard her use: "My name is Tamsin Roake. I'm bell-master of the Meridian Gull. I'd like to speak to Ysolde Kerrin, if she's here, and if she isn't I'll wait, and if you'd rather we went back up we'll go back up. We're not the Company. There's no Company on this boat."
The man's lamp steadied a little.
"You're Tamsin," he said.
"I am."

"She said you'd come." He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "She's said it every year since I was a boy. Every midsummer, when we ring the long one, she says: one of these years Tamsin Roake is going to work it out and come down that ladder, and when she does, mind your manners, because she'll have earned it."
They walked up through the town, and Sol looked at everything, and everything she looked at rearranged something in her head.

A school. Eleven children in it, at that hour, because school on Lowspire ran at night when the air was still. A chandler's shop with four items in the window and all four of them clean. A chapel that had plainly been two chapels once and had been made into one by the simple expedient of knocking a wall down, which suggested a story Sol wanted very badly to hear.
A washing line with a child's shirt on it, and a woman taking it in, and the woman stopped with the shirt in her hands and stared at Sol's uniform with her mouth open.

And under everything, felt in the soles of the feet rather than heard, the long steady hum of a bell that had been rung true a quarter of an hour ago and would be rung true again in eight hours, holding four hundred feet of iron and two hundred and eleven people in the air over a cinder-cliff.
Sol stopped in the middle of the street.
"Bosun," she said.
"I know."
"They're standing on our carry."
"I know," said Roake. "Keep walking. And Ferrant — get your face in order. Whatever we do about this, we do not do it while looking at these people as if they were a sum."
The thing Sol could not get past was the quiet.

Not silence — Lowspire was not silent; there were voices, and a hand-loom going somewhere, and the small constant noise of two hundred people living on four hundred feet of platform. It was that every noise on that platform had been made small on purpose. Doors were eased shut. Buckets were set down rather than dropped. A man came past with a barrow and Sol realised, after he had gone, that the barrow had rags bound round the rim of its wheel.
She said so to the man with the lamp, whose name turned out to be Wren Beck — the engineer's son, born on the platform, forty years old and the nearest thing Lowspire had to a mayor.

"Vibration bleeds carry," he said, as if reciting a table. "Bleeds it faster than you would think. My father worked it out in the first year, when we were dropping a foot a week. Everything that shakes costs us height."
"So you stopped everything that shakes."
"We stopped everything we could and we slowed everything we couldn't." He shrugged. "Children learn it at four. There's a rhyme for it."
"Say it."
He looked embarrassed, and then he said it, in the flat sing-song of a thing learned before memory:

Soft on the boards and soft on the stair,
soft with the door and the pail and the chair.
Loud is a shilling and shillings are dear,
and the ones who were loud are no longer here.
Sol stood in the middle of a street in a town in the sky and did not trust herself to speak for some time.
"That last line," she managed.
"Aye," said Wren Beck. "That one's not about vibration."

chapters.title: Chapter Fifteen: Ysolde Kerrin

blocks.c: Chapter Fifteen: Ysolde Kerrin

She was in the bell-house, of course, because where else would she be, and she was cleaning the sound-bow with a rag and a paste of chalk and oil, exactly as Roake did on the Gull, exactly as Roake had taught Sol to do, and the sight of the same four motions performed by a stranger's hands made the whole eleven years fold up like a chart.

Ysolde Kerrin was seventy-one. She was tall, and had been taller. She wore a bell-master's leather over a miner's coat, and when she turned round she looked at the four of them and did not look surprised, and Sol thought: she has been rehearsing this for eleven years and she is about to be very good at it, and I must not let that count for anything.
"Tamsin," said Kerrin.
"Ysolde."
"You look well."
"I look sixty. You look older than the hills and you're cleaning that bow wrong; you always did. You go with the grain of the metal, not across it."
Kerrin's face broke into a smile so genuine that Sol felt an unwilling tug of liking, and hated it.
"There," said the old woman. "That's my girl. Twenty-two years and the first thing out of her mouth is a correction." She put down the rag. "Who are the others?"
"Company observer," said Sallow, "and I'd be glad if you'd all stop saying that as if it were a disease."
"Frames," said Dov.
"Third-watch hand," said Sol.
Kerrin looked at her for a moment longer than at the others.
"You're the ear," she said.
"How do you know that?"

"Because you came in and looked at the bell before you looked at me, and because you've got your head tipped four degrees to the left, which is what a hand does when she's listening to a room." Kerrin picked up her rag again. "Also because a man in a good coat has been sending me letters about you for a month."
Every head in the bell-house turned.
Sallow, to his credit, did not attempt to look innocent. He took his hat off and turned it round in his hands.
"Well," he said. "Yes."
The story took an hour and Kerrin told it standing up, which Sol came to understand was a kind of courtesy: she was not going to make it comfortable for herself.
The platform was cut loose in seventy-eight. The notice went up in Fourthmonth. Eleven shillings a ticket, and no credit, and no exceptions, and a Company agent at the head of the lift to check them.

"Two hundred and forty stayed," said Kerrin. "Not out of heroism. Out of arithmetic. A man with four children and no shillings cannot buy five tickets, and he will not buy one, and so he does not buy any, and the Company writes down nil."

Lowspire had lasted eleven months on the carry left in its frame. It had gone down eleven feet in the first four, and then more slowly, because the platform's own engineer, a man called Beck, had worked out that if you stopped every hammer and every cart and every source of vibration on the whole structure, the carry drained slower.
"Eleven months of a town on tiptoe," said Kerrin. "The children learned to walk quietly before they learned to run. Then Beck died and I came down."
"With a bell," said Roake.

"With a bell that was sitting in a locked cupboard on a ship, doing nothing, made from the same melt as one being rung four times a day, four beats flat, by a woman I had trained myself and who I knew would go on ringing it four beats flat for the rest of her life." Kerrin's chin came up. "Yes. With a bell. And I have rung it true, twice a day, every day, for eleven years, and I have taken about one part in a hundred of the Meridian Gull's carry, and with it I have held two hundred and eleven people in the air."
"Two hundred and forty," said Sol.
"Two hundred and forty stayed," said Ysolde Kerrin. "Two hundred and eleven are here. I said the first eleven months were slow. I did not say they were kind."
Nobody spoke for a while. Outside the bell-house a dog barked, and someone shushed it, out of a habit eleven years old.
"You could have asked," said Roake, at last, and her voice cracked straight down the middle. "Ysolde. You could have come up that lift and stood on the wharf and asked me."
"Asked you for what, Tamsin? For a part in a hundred? You didn't have it to give. It isn't yours; it's the Company's, and the Company had already written nil in a book."
"You could have asked me."

"Yes," said Kerrin. "And you would have said yes, and they would have taken your papers, and then you would have been a woman with no papers standing on a wharf, and there would be two hundred and eleven fewer people in the world." She turned back to her bell. "I did not steal your carry, girl. I stole your choice. That is the part I would give back if I could, and I can't, and I have not lost a night's sleep over it, and you may make of that what you like."
Sol had promised herself she would keep out of it. She lasted nine more seconds.
"You took it off four ships," she said.
Kerrin's rag stopped.
"Say that again."

"Four ships. The fleet's coal went up four per cent the year after the Gull's refit and it never came back down. Only ours shows in a tally, because only ours is paired, but the carry over this stretch of the Cloudsea has been thin for eleven years and everybody's been paying for it in coal and calling it the price of the season." Sol's heart was going hard. "You didn't steal from a Company, ma'am. You stole from four crews who ring four flat because nobody ever told them any different, and every one of them has been quietly worse at their job for eleven years and doesn't know why."
The bell-house was very quiet.
"Yes," said Ysolde Kerrin at last. "That is true, and I did not know it, and I should have. Write it down."
"Ma'am?"

"You heard me. Get a pen and write it down and put it in your tally, in the margin, in your own hand, so that when they come to make the case there is a line in a book that says the bell-master of Lowspire was told a thing she had not accounted for and did not argue." She turned back to the bow, and her voice, for the first time, was old. "I have kept a very careful book for eleven years, girl. It is the only thing I have left that is honest. Do not let me spoil it now by being proud in front of a child."

chapters.title: Chapter Sixteen: The Town That Has to Be Rung

blocks.c: Chapter Sixteen: The Town That Has to Be Rung
They stayed nineteen hours, because the Sprat could not go up until the Gull came round again, and because — Sol suspected — Roake could not have got back in that boat if she had tried.
Sol spent the hours walking, and Lowspire let her.

She learned that the town rang twice a day: a full round at the sixth hour and a short round at the eighteenth, and that the whole population knew both by heart, and that the rounds were rung by four hands in rotation, all of them trained by Kerrin, the youngest of whom was nineteen and had been born on the platform.

She learned that the carry was rationed like water. Every hammer blow on the platform was logged. There was a smith, but the smith worked only in the four hours after a round, when the carry was at its fullest, because vibration bleeds it. There was a school but no bell in the school. There were two hundred and eleven people and not one dog with a loud bark; the dogs were selected for it, which was the single most unsettling fact Sol learned all day.

She learned that they had a tally. Of course they had a tally. It was kept in the chapel because that was the driest building, and it went back eleven years, and the marks were in four hands, and it was as thick as her fist.

She read a page of it standing up and found the eleven long rounds — the midsummer takings, the ones that had shown as dead on the Gull's book — and beside each, in Kerrin's writing, the same four words:
Taken. Recorded. Owed. Sorry.
Eleven times. The same four words. Sol stood in a cold chapel with her thumb on the page for a long time.
The school was in the chapel too, and school on Lowspire ran at night, and Sol got herself invited into it by the simple method of standing in the doorway until somebody took pity on her.

There were eleven children, aged four to fifteen, and one teacher, a woman called Ottilie who had been a governess in Antrell in another life and had come down the Low Stair in eighty-four for reasons Sol never learned. The lesson was arithmetic. The arithmetic was carry.

That was the thing that stopped her in the doorway. In Kettlemouth, a child of nine learns sums with apples and shillings. Here, a girl of about eight was standing at a slate working out how many hours of hold a short round buys in still air against a load of two hundred tons, and getting it right, and being corrected on her handwriting rather than her answer.

"They all learn it," said Ottilie afterwards. "They have to. There is no one else. If the four hands are ill at once, somebody has to be able to ring, and somebody has to be able to tell them whether it worked."
"Can they? Tell whether it worked?"

"Three of them can. Pel is nineteen and rings the sixth-hour round on his own. Marta is eleven and I think will be better than him." Ottilie looked at Sol with a sudden and unnerving directness. "You are the ear off the ferry."
"Yes."

"Then may I ask you something I have wanted to ask a qualified person for nine years?" She lowered her voice. "Is it bad for them? Growing up on a hold. Hearing it all the time, in the feet, day and night, from birth. Does it do anything?"
Sol opened her mouth to say no, and found that she did not know, and that nobody in the world knew, because nobody in the world had ever grown up on a platform held in the air by a bell.
"I don't know," she said. "I'd like to find out. I'd like to find out with them here rather than not here, if that's all right."
Ottilie laughed for the first time. "That," she said, "is the least reassuring reassurance I have ever been given, and the first honest one, so thank you."
Dov, meanwhile, had gone under the platform, because that is what Dov did, and came up grey to the eyebrows and unusually quiet.
"Tell me," said Sol.
"The frame's got four years in it. Maybe five."
"Four years of what?"

"Of metal. Not carry — metal." He sat down on a bollard. "Carry holds it up. Fine. But the whole structure is cinder-iron out of the local seam, and cinder-iron rots when it's held under load in wet air, and they are four hundred feet under a cloud, which is the wettest air in the world. Every stringer I put a pick into came away in flakes. They have been so careful about vibration for eleven years that nobody has noticed the frame is going soft."
"Can it be fixed?"

"Yes. It needs about two hundred tons of good iron, a forge that can run all day, and eleven months of hammering." Dov looked up at her. "Hammering, Sol. On a platform where a smith works four hours a day because a hammer bleeds the carry."
Sol sat down slowly on the bollard beside him.
"So they can't repair it," she said, "because repairing it would drop them."

"They can't repair it on the carry they steal. It's not enough. It has never been enough; it's exactly enough to stay still, which is the worst possible amount." He rubbed his face and made it worse. "Kerrin's been running the finest piece of engineering I have ever seen in my life for eleven years and she has built a machine whose only output is standing still, and in four years it comes apart, and I do not think she knows."

Sol thought about the chalk on the inside of a door, and the four words in the chapel tally, and a woman of seventy-one cleaning a sound-bow across the grain because she had nobody left to correct her.
"She knows," she said.

chapters.title: Chapter Seventeen: Terms

blocks.c: Chapter Seventeen: Terms
Ivor Sallow made his offer in the chapel, at a trestle table, with the chapel's tally at his elbow, and he made it well, which was the trouble.

"I represent eleven people," he said. "Not the Company; the Company is a word. Eleven people own the run, and of those eleven, four are old and frightened and seven would sell their mothers for a percentage. I have spent nineteen years learning which is which, and I have spent the last four buying the debts of the four."
"You want the run," said Roake.

"I want the run to be worth having in twenty years, which is not the same thing and is much harder." Sallow spread his hands on the table. "Here is what happens now if I do nothing. In forty days the probation ends. The Gull will have had three good crossings, because Miss Ferrant has found a tenth of a beat and the carry is up, and the commissioners will write down that the deficiency has resolved itself, and the file will close, and in four years the frame under this platform comes apart in the night and two hundred and eleven people go into a cinder-cliff, and nobody will ever know they were here, because the Company's number is nil."
The chapel was very quiet.

"And here is what happens if I tell the truth," he went on. "I lay the tally, the coal ledger, the pour book and Miss Ferrant's margins on that table in Antrell and I say: this platform has been stealing carry from a passenger vessel for eleven years. Do you know what the Company does then? It does not send help. It sends a bell-wright with a warrant, and it takes that bell, and the theft stops, and the platform goes down in a season instead of four years, and every one of those eleven owners sleeps perfectly well, because the notice was posted in seventy-eight and everyone had a chance to buy a ticket."
"You're saying the truth kills them," said Sol.
"I'm saying the truth, said in that room, in that order, kills them." Sallow turned his hat round in his hands. "So I propose we say it in a different order."
The offer had four parts and Dov wrote them on a slate as they came.

items: Lowspire is declared, not discovered. Sallow files a claim on a lapsed mineral lease in the name of a company he already owns, and the platform becomes a working station with a legal existence, two hundred and eleven employees, and a mail contract.
The Meridian Gull is contracted to serve it. Not to give carry away — to be paid for it. One call a crossing, on the down leg, tender to the platform, mail and stores and iron.

The theft becomes a supply. The tenth bell is licensed as a pair, which requires an act of the Bellwrights' Company and which Sallow claims, with the confidence of a man who has bought four debts, to be able to obtain.

In exchange, Sallow's company takes the platform's cinder-iron seam, which is not dead, whatever the Company wrote in seventy-eight, and which he has had a man sampling for four years, and which is worth an amount of money he declined to say out loud in a chapel.

blocks.c: "There it is," he said. "I am not a good man, Bosun. I am a man who has found a way for the profitable thing and the decent thing to be the same thing, which is the most any of us manage, and I intend to be paid for it."
Roake read the slate twice.
"What do you need from us?" she said.

"Three things. A bell-master of standing to certify that a licensed pair can be rung safely on one run — which no one will believe from me and everyone will believe from you. A ship's officer to log the calls, which means Captain Marn's signature and therefore his neck. And an ear." He looked at Sol. "Because the whole scheme rests on the double round, and nobody has ever rung one, and if it cannot be rung then all I have is a nice idea and a lease."
"What's a double round?" said Dov.

"A round that pays two towns," said Sol, and discovered that she had already been thinking about it for nineteen hours without admitting it. "Nine bells up here holding the ship, and a tenth down there holding the platform, and both of them rung so that neither is stealing from the other."
"Can it be done?" said Sallow.
Sol looked at Kerrin, who had not said one word since the offer began, and who was standing at the back of the chapel with her arms folded and her face like the side of a hill.
"Ysolde," said Sol. "Can it be done?"
The old woman took a long breath.

"I have had eleven years and a bell and nothing else to think about," she said, "and yes, it can be done, and it wants a hand at each end who can hold four and one within a hair, and there is no such pair of hands in the world."
"There's yours," said Roake.
"There's mine at seventy-one, with an arm that goes numb after the fourth strike."
"Then train one," said Sol.
Every head in the chapel turned to her, and she discovered that she had stood up at some point without deciding to.

"You said there's no such pair of hands in the world. There isn't, because nobody has ever needed one, because nobody has ever rung a double round. There was no such thing as a person who could ring four and one either, until you chalked it on a door." She was talking too fast and let herself. "You've got four hands down here and a girl of eleven in that school who Ottilie says will be better than Pel. We've got two hands on the Gull who can hold four flat all day and a bell-master with twenty-two years. That's seven people and a schoolroom. Give me a season."
"We have four years," said Dov, quietly, "not a season," and then, when everybody looked at him: "The frame. I have not told you about the frame yet."
He told them about the frame.

It took nine minutes and at the end of it the chapel was silent in the particular way of a room in which everybody has just been given the same piece of arithmetic and is checking it privately, hoping to find an error.
"Four years," said Wren Beck.

"Four to five. It's not a cliff. It goes soft and then it goes." Dov spread his hands. "And you cannot fix it, because fixing it is eleven months of hammering, and hammering bleeds carry, and you do not have carry to bleed. You have exactly enough to stand still. That is what makes it a trap rather than a problem."
"Then there's mine," said Roake.
"Yes," said Kerrin, and for the first time she looked at her old apprentice with something naked in her face. "There's yours. That is what I have been afraid of for eleven years."

chapters.title: Chapter Eighteen: Mutiny Is a Strong Word

blocks.c: Chapter Eighteen: Mutiny Is a Strong Word
Captain Ovid Marn said no.

He said it courteously, at length, with reasons, in the chart room, standing up, and Sol — who had spent the entire return flight rehearsing arguments — found that she had not prepared for reasons that were good.

"I have four hundred and eleven passengers," he said. "I have a probation with thirty-one days to run and a Company observer whom you now tell me is running a private commercial scheme out of my chart room. You are asking me to take an unlicensed tender below the cloudline, on a schedule, into dead air, on the strength of an interval which was chalked on a door by a woman who is in breach of eleven statutes, and to log it truthfully, which will end my career, or falsely, which will end it faster and worse."
"Yes, sir," said Sol.
"And your answer to all of that is yes, sir?"
"My answer is that they're there, sir, and in four years they won't be."
Marn turned to the window. The cloud went past.
"Bosun," he said. "Your view."
"My view is that the girl is right and that you should say no anyway," said Roake.
Sol's head came round so fast her neck cracked.

"Because if you say yes," Roake went on, "you'll do it as a captain, which means orders, which means logs, which means that when it goes wrong — and the first one will go wrong, Ovid, they always do — it goes wrong on the ship's book, and they take the Gull off the run, and then there is no ferry at all and everybody drowns in the air together." She put her hands flat on the chart table. "Say no. Say it loudly. Put it in the log. And then be somewhere else for eleven minutes at the turn of the third watch, and do not ask what the bell-master and her hand are doing on the gallery, because bell-masters have rung experimental rounds without asking permission since before this Company existed, and there is a word for it, and the word is not mutiny, the word is trade practice."
There was a long silence.
"That," said Marn, "is the most disgraceful thing I have ever heard said in this room."
"Yes, sir."
"How long have you been saving it?"
"Twenty-two years, sir."
Marn looked at the ceiling for a while.

"The turn of the third watch," he said, "is when I take my exercise on the after deck. It takes me eleven minutes. I am extremely regular about it and I would thank everyone in this room to stop looking at me."
So they rang the first double round without permission, in the dark, four miles north of the Quiet, on the sixth night out.

The Sprat went down with Kerrin's youngest hand aboard — a nineteen-year-old called Pel who had never in his life been above the cloudline and who spent the first four minutes of the descent looking up instead of down. He carried a repeater: a light iron rod strung with wire, an instrument Dov had built in nineteen hours out of a spare stay and a broken frame, which did nothing at all except hum when the Gull's Ninth was struck true, and which would let a hand four hundred feet below hear the ship's count.
Roake had the hammer on the Gull. Sol had the frame.
Keel. Ladder. Kestrel. Quarrel. Mother. Lantern. Thimble. Widow.

Four and one. Four and one. Four and one, and Roake's arms moving with the awful economy of twenty-two years, and each bell coming up full, and the carry laying down over the ship like a hand smoothing a sheet.
And then the Ninth, and the hold, and the count of nine — and, from four hundred feet below, arriving up through the frames of a ship in the dark, the twin.

It was the most beautiful thing Sol Ferrant had ever heard in her life and she had no words for it then and never found any afterwards. Two bells from one melt, forty-one years apart, holding one note between them across four hundred feet of wet air, and neither of them taking it from the other, because the interval was true.
Dov, at the frame, said in a small voice: "Carry's up. Both. Both of them are up."
Roake stood at the stern with the hammer hanging from her hand and tears running straight down her face and no expression on it whatsoever.
"Ferrant," she said. "Tally."
Sol wrote it. And under the ninth column, in the margin, she wrote the tenth.

They talked about it for nineteen days afterwards and never got it right, which Sol eventually decided was the correct outcome, because a thing you can describe completely is a thing you have finished with.

Dov's version was mechanical and beautiful and about eleven pages long, and it introduced a word — coupling — that four other lines were using within three years, and it never once mentioned what the round sounded like, because Dov had been lying on his back under a lift-frame with his eyes shut and had genuinely not noticed.

Sallow's version was two sentences long and went in a letter to a man in Antrell who owned eleven per cent of a ferry line: The pair can be rung without loss to either party. I require your proxy at the winter meeting.
Kerrin's version, sent up on the Sprat in a hand that shook more than it had eleven years ago, was four words: You leaned on it.
Roake's version was the one Sol kept.
The bosun wrote it in the tally itself, at the bottom of the page, out of the columns, in the free margin, in handwriting that had been getting worse for twenty-two years:

First double round. Ship and station. Both up. Neither took. Interval four and one, held by Roake above and by a boy below whose name I did not have when I began writing this line and now do: Pel Anwar, nineteen, of Lowspire, who has never been above the cloud in his life and rang the truest ninth I have heard in thirty years. Recommend he be examined for his ticket at Antrell at the Company's expense. Recommend the Company be given no choice in the matter.

chapters.title: Chapter Nineteen: The Cracked Bell

blocks.c: Chapter Nineteen: The Cracked Bell
They rang eleven double rounds over nine days and every one of them worked, and that is why nobody was ready.

You get used to things. That is the whole of it. By the fourth crossing the double round had a rota; by the sixth it had a shorthand; by the ninth, Cook Anselm was sending a hamper down on the Sprat because someone had mentioned that there were children on the platform who had never eaten an orange, and the whole business had acquired the awful comfortable feeling of a thing that is simply how it is done now.
Sol had even begun to be bored during the descent, which she recognised, in retrospect, as the exact moment the trade stops keeping you alive.
There had been warnings. There are always warnings; the trouble is that a warning and a nothing look identical until afterwards.

items: On the seventh round the Ninth's tail had come back a hair short, and Sol had marked it thin and rung again and got it full and thought no more about it.

On the ninth, Roake had run her thumb round the crown after the round and stood there with her head on one side for four seconds longer than usual, and had said nothing, because there was nothing to say that a tally would accept.

On the tenth, Dov had reported a change in the frame note under load and had written it up and filed it, and it had gone into the pile of things to look at in Antrell, along with a sticking valve and a door that would not shut.

blocks.c: Nobody was careless. That is the part Sol needed people to understand afterwards, and never once managed to say without sounding as though she were making excuses. A bell of forty-one years that has been rung four times a day at an interval a tenth of a beat wrong has been very slightly hurt on every single one of those strikes, sixty thousand times, and then one day it is rung correctly and the correct blow is the one that finds the fault.
They had fixed the count. The count was what killed it.
On the eleventh, coming up on the Quiet in a wind off the north with a squall line running ahead of it, the Ninth cracked.

It did not shatter. Bells almost never do. What happened was that Roake struck a true blow on a bell that had been rung four times a day for eleven years with a tenth of a beat missing from its count, and forty-one years of stress in the crown found a fault the size of a hair and travelled eleven inches along it in about a thousandth of a second.

The sound it made was not loud. It was worse than loud. It was a note that started and then went wrong in the middle, a bright ringing thing turning into a flat, buzzing, meat-like noise, and Sol, with her hand on the frame, felt the carry go out from under the whole ship like a floor being taken away.
"Off!" Roake screamed. "Hammer off! Nobody strike it!"
The Gull went down eleven spans in nineteen seconds.
What that is like is this.

The lamps swing and the shadows all run one way. The deck is not soft now; the deck is gone, and you are standing on a thing that is falling at the same speed you are, which is the definition of a floor you cannot use. Somewhere below there is the noise of four hundred and eleven people all being frightened in one place, which is a sound no one who has heard it ever describes properly.

Sol was on her knees with her fingers through the frame grating. Dov was hanging off the ballast lever with both feet off the deck. Roake was already at Keel with the hammer up, ringing the fall-off — Keel, Mother, Widow, four beats, four beats — and the three deep bells were doing what three deep bells can do, which is not enough.
"Eight bells won't hold her!" Dov shouted. "We're eleven under and the frames are cold!"
"Then get me the ninth!" Roake shouted back.
"It's cracked!"
"I know it's cracked!"

And then, in the middle of that, from below the keel line, from four hundred feet down in the dark where a nineteen-year-old with a repeater and a bell had just heard his ship's ninth bell die: the twin.

It rang alone. Out of round, out of sequence, against every rule in the trade — a bell struck by itself with nothing to lean on — and Sol felt the pull come up through the deck and turn, unmistakably, into a push.
"He's giving it back," she said.
"What?"
"Pel. He's ringing the tenth to hold us. He's spending their carry on us."
Roake's head came round.
"How long can he hold it?"
Sol did the sum with a mouth that had gone completely dry.
"Until their frame goes," she said.

And then, because there was no time to be gentle about it: "Bosun, he's nineteen and he's alone in a bell-house and he can feel our carry through the plinth. He knows exactly what he's doing and he'll do it until the platform goes soft under him, because he can hear four hundred and eleven people up here and he cannot hear two hundred and eleven behind him, and that is how anybody makes that decision."
Roake shut her eyes for precisely one beat.
"Then we take it back off him," she said, "before he gives us all of it."
"With what? We've got eight bells and a cracked ninth."
"We have got eight bells, a cracked ninth, and a hush." Roake was already moving down the line. "Get it."

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty: Tamsin's Last Round

blocks.c: Chapter Twenty: Tamsin's Last Round
There is a thing bell-hands are told and do not believe, which is that a cracked bell can be rung.

Not safely. Not twice. A cracked bell will give you one true tail if you strike it exactly right — on the sound-bow, square, at the one point on the circumference where the fault is not — and it will hum for perhaps eleven seconds, and then the crack will run the rest of the way and the bell will be scrap and the sound will come out of it in a way that no ear should be within twenty feet of.
Roake sent Sol for the plate.

It was in the bell-master's cubby, under the tally: a curved iron plate on a chain, the width of a hand, four hundred years old, called a hush. You clamp it over the crack to hold the metal together for the length of one strike. Every ship carried one. Nobody had used one in living memory. Sol had been shown it once, at thirteen, along with the fire buckets and the ballast wrench, in the tour where you are shown all the things that mean everything has gone wrong.

She came back up the nineteen rungs with the plate in her teeth, and on the way she passed a steward going down with an armful of blankets, and the steward said something to her that she did not hear, and she thought afterwards that it had probably been good luck, and that she should have answered.
That is what those minutes were like. Everybody doing their own small correct thing in a ship that was going down, and none of it adding up to enough, and all of it necessary.

The Gull was down thirty-one spans and falling slower, held on three deep bells and a stolen twin, and the cloud-tops were no longer below them; they were level, and coming past the gallery in long grey fingers.
"Give it here," said Roake.
"Bosun—"
"Ferrant, give me the plate."
"You'll be next to it."
"Yes."
"You'll be a foot from it when it goes—"
"Yes," said Tamsin Roake, and took the hush out of her hands.
She clamped it. She checked it with her thumb, twice, the way she checked everything, and Sol saw her mouth moving and could not hear a word over the wind.
"Ferrant. Off the gallery."
"No."
"That was not a request, it was an order, and I am the bell-master."

"And I'm the ear," said Sol, "and if that hush slips a hair you'll not know it and I will, and I can shout at you from the number-eight cradle, which is eleven feet, which is further than you're going to be." Her voice was doing something appalling. "Bosun, please. Let me be useful. Don't make me be a witness."
Tamsin Roake looked at her for about a second and a half, which in the circumstances was an enormous extravagance.
"Number-eight cradle," she said. "Behind the yoke. Hands over your ears from the ninth strike and do not take them down for anything."

Then Roake looked down the line of nine bells — eight good and one dying — and she did the thing that Sol thought about every day for the rest of her life, which was that she took the time to walk the line and touch each cradle, in order, bow to stern, the superstition that everyone on that ship pretended not to have.
Then she rang the round.
Keel, low and enormous. Ladder. Kestrel. Quarrel. Mother, taking her breath and then saying everything at once. Lantern. Thimble. Widow, sour and reliable.
Four and one. Four and one. Not one strike out.

And at the stern, with her left hand flat on the hush and her right on the hammer, at a distance from a failing bell that no bell-master in four hundred years had survived and gone on hearing, Tamsin Roake struck the Ninth of the Meridian Gull.
It rang true.

It rang true for eleven seconds, and in those eleven seconds Sol Ferrant felt the carry come back into the frame under her hands like water into a dry channel, felt the whole eight hundred tons of the ship stop arguing with the sky and lie down on it, felt the Gull come up four spans, then four more; and four hundred feet below, a nineteen-year-old called Pel, whose town had eleven seconds of carry left in it, heard his ship's ninth bell speak and knew he could stop.
Then the crack ran.

The noise that came out of the Ninth was not a sound. Sol was eleven feet away and she went down on the plating with her hands over her ears and it did not help; it came through her forearms. Dov, at the frame, was knocked flat. The hush plate tore off its chain and went out over the rail into the cloud and was never found.
And Tamsin Roake, one foot from the bell she had kept for twenty-two years, did not move at all until it was over.

The Gull came up nineteen spans in four minutes and levelled at thirty-one, and the squall went over the top of her and away south, and four hundred and eleven passengers were told by a purser of forty-one years' standing that there had been an incident with a bell, that the ship was safe, that the bar would be open and free until Antrell, and that anybody who wished to make a complaint should address it to him personally and in writing, which is the single most effective method ever devised for reducing the number of complaints.

She was standing when Sol got to her. Standing, with her hand still on the hammer, looking at the ruined bell with a kind of professional sorrow, and when Sol grabbed her arm she turned round and her face was perfectly calm.
Sol was shouting. She knew she was shouting. She could hear herself shouting.
Roake watched her mouth for a moment. Then she reached out and put her palm flat against Sol's breastbone, over the sternum, where the underhum lives, and held it there.
"Don't shout," she said, far too loudly, in the voice of a person who cannot hear their own voice. "It doesn't work anymore."
She looked past Sol, down the line of bells, at eight good iron hearts and one dead one, and at a ship that was rising.
"Ferrant," said the bell-master of the Meridian Gull. "Tally."

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-One: The Double Round

blocks.c: Chapter Twenty-One: The Double Round

They came into Kettlemouth on eight bells, four days late, with a dead Ninth lashed in its cradle under a tarpaulin like a body, and the whole harbour turned out to watch, because a ring-ship coming in low is the best free entertainment in the world.
Sol rang every round of those four days. There was nobody else.

That is not quite true — there were two other hands aboard, both competent, both able to hold four beats and neither able to hold four and one, and after the second watch they came to her separately and said the same thing in different words, which was: you take it, we'll do the frames. It was the least dramatic promotion in the history of the trade and it happened in a galley over cold tea.

She rang. She wrote the tally. She slept in pieces. She learned, in four days, the thing that Roake had never once said out loud: that being the person who holds a ship up is not a feeling of power at all, it is the feeling of being a shelf.
And twice a day, four hundred feet below and eleven miles behind, a town rang with her.
The first call after the crack was the worst hour of the whole affair, and it did not have a single dramatic thing in it.

The Sprat went down with Sol, Dov, four hundredweight of iron rod, a bag of mail, and Cook Anselm's hamper, and Sol spent the descent trying to work out how to tell two hundred and eleven people that the ship they were now legally, publicly and permanently attached to had just proved it could drop thirty-one spans without warning.

She need not have bothered. They already knew. They had felt it: the pull, then the surge, then the eleven seconds of a bell rung by a woman with her hand on a crack, and then the awful slack afterwards while Pel held them both.
Wren Beck was on the landing stage. So was most of the town.
"Is she alive?" he said, before the boat was fast.
"She's alive. She's deaf."
Beck absorbed that. Behind him somebody made a small noise.
"And the bell?"

"Scrap. They'll recast it in the spring." Sol got out onto the stage and found her legs did not want to be stood on. "Mister Beck, I have to say something and I'd rather say it once, to everyone, and then never again."
"Say it, then."
So she stood on a mail crate on a landing stage under a cloud and said it to two hundred people.

"Your carry and ours are the same carry now. That means when we're in trouble you'll feel it, and when you're in trouble we'll feel it, and neither of us gets to pretend otherwise ever again. Four nights ago a nineteen-year-old in your bell-house spent your height to hold my ship up and I am not going to stand here and thank him for it, because thanking him would mean it was a favour, and it wasn't. It was the arrangement. It works both ways or it doesn't work."
There was a silence.
Then a woman near the back said, "Did the oranges come?" and everybody laughed, including Sol, until she had to sit down on the crate she had been standing on.
The double round became a schedule because Dov made it one, and Dov made it one because he had discovered, in the middle of the worst night of his life, that he was good at exactly this.
Here is the schedule they ran that autumn, and it is worth setting down, because it was copied afterwards by four other lines and nobody ever credited an engineer's apprentice of seventeen.

items: On the down leg, four miles north of the Quiet, the Gull rings her round at four and one, and the platform rings the twin on the count of nine. Both are up. Neither takes.

On the up leg, the platform rings alone at the sixth hour, and the Gull rings a short round two watches later, which lays a fresh carry over the same air. The platform drinks the surplus. This is the part nobody had thought of, and it is Kerrin's, and she worked it out in about eleven seconds when Dov described the problem.
The Sprat calls once a crossing with mail, stores and iron. Iron every time. Two tons a call, which is nothing, which over eleven months is enough to begin a frame.

Everything is logged. On the ship's tally, in the chapel tally, and in a third book kept by Sallow's company, in triplicate, because the entire scheme's protection is that it is boring and well documented.

blocks.c: "Boring is the point," Sallow said, when Sol complained about the paperwork. "A thing that is exciting gets stopped. A thing that is in triplicate becomes a procedure, and a procedure is the safest place in the world to hide two hundred and eleven people."
Teaching four and one turned out to be the hardest thing Sol had ever attempted, and she attempted it on eleven people at once.

The four flat hands could not feel the tenth. That was the whole difficulty. You cannot count a tenth of a beat; there is nothing there to count; the interval is shorter than the smallest thing a human being can deliberately do. Sol worked at it for a month and got nowhere, and then in Kettlemouth, standing at the gate of a rope yard in the rain, she got it, and it had nothing to do with counting at all.

"Stop trying to be late," she told them, the next morning, on the gallery, with two ship's hands and a bosun who read her lips. "You're all trying to add a bit on to the four. You can't. Nobody can. So don't. Ring the four — and lean into the bell as you strike, the way you lean into a door you think is locked. That's it. That's the whole trick. The lean puts the tenth in your arm and the arm puts it in the bell."
The younger hand got it in nine minutes. The older one took four days and then never lost it again.

Roake, who could not hear a single note of any of it, stood with her palm flat on the number-eight cradle and marked every strike full or thin by feel alone, and was right every time, and afterwards said, on her slate:
I have been ringing a tenth of a beat wrong for twenty-two years and it took a deaf woman to certify the correction. Put that in your report, Mister Sallow, and I hope it keeps you up at night.

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Two: What It Costs to Hold

blocks.c: Chapter Twenty-Two: What It Costs to Hold
Tamsin Roake did not go deaf all at once, which everyone had assumed she had.

What she had lost, the surgeon at Antrell said, was the high end and most of the middle, permanently and comprehensively, on both sides. She could hear a shout as a kind of pressure. She could hear Mother, the deepest bell but one, as a sensation in the chest. She could not hear a voice, or a bell tail, or her own footsteps, and never would again.
She was fifty-nine years old and had been the best ear on the run for thirty of them.

The Company offered her a pension at two thirds and a cottage at Antrell with a view of the ridge, and it was, Halloway said, a genuinely decent offer by the standards of an institution that had written nil in a book for eleven years.
Roake read the letter twice and wrote four words on her slate and turned it round.
I am not finished.

Sol went with her to the surgeon and stood in the corridor afterwards and cried in the ugly, undignified, hiccuping way she had not done since she was eleven, and Roake waited it out, and then wrote on the slate she now carried everywhere:
Stop that. I can still feel a round through the deck. That is more than most people get, and I intend to be extremely annoying about it.
The reckoning at Antrell took a month and went the way Sallow had said it would, which is to say: badly, then boringly, then well.

The badly was the first week. A ring-ship had lost thirty-one spans with four hundred and eleven souls aboard, and there was a bell in scrap, and the Company wanted a person to be at fault, and the person available was a captain who had written, in his own log, in his own hand, on the night of the crack: Bell-master and third-watch hand engaged in an experimental round below the cloudline. Not ordered by me. Not prevented by me.
Marn had done it deliberately. Sol found that out later. He could have written nothing at all.

The boringly was the next three weeks, and it was Halloway's doing, and Sol had never respected anybody so much in her life. The purser arrived at the commission with the tally, the coal ledgers for eleven years, the pour book from the Foundry, Ottring's sworn statement about melt sixty-two, Dov's arithmetic in fair copy, a lease claim filed by a company nobody had heard of, a mail contract, and two hundred and eleven names.
Names. He had gone down on the Sprat himself and taken them, one at a time, with ages, trades and birthplaces, in his very small neat hand.
"You cannot write nil," he told the commission, "in the presence of a list."
The well was the finding, in Elevenmonth, which nobody read out loud because it ran to forty pages and was mostly about lease boundaries. Its substance was four things:

items: The Lowspire Platform Station was recognised as a working station of the Antrell run, with a mail contract and a licensed pair, the second such licence granted in ninety years.
The Meridian Gull was returned to full service, her probation discharged, with a standing order to call at the station once each crossing.
Captain Ovid Marn was censured for permitting an unauthorised round and commended for the conduct of his ship during the settling, in the same paragraph, which he had framed.

Ysolde Kerrin, of no fixed address, was found to have committed a continuing theft of carry over eleven years, and was fined a sum of money she did not have, and was appointed bell-master of the station she had stolen it for, at a salary from which the fine would be deducted, over a period of four hundred and eleven years.

blocks.c: "They enjoyed that," said Sallow. "Commissions have a sense of humour about once a decade and I am glad I was there for it."

Sol asked Kerrin about it, on the platform, in the spring, with the new iron going up on the north frame and the sound of hammers ringing out for eleven hours a day because there was carry enough now to spend on repair.
"Do you regret it?"
"Which part?"
"Any of it. The bell. The eleven years. Not asking."
Ysolde Kerrin, who was seventy-two and looked it, watched two men swing a stringer into place.
"I regret the interval," she said.
"The interval?"

"Four and one. I had it in eleven days. I chalked it on a door in a locked cupboard on a ship and told nobody, because it was mine and because I was going to need it." She flexed her bad hand. "If I had walked up to the ring gallery in Fourthmonth of seventy-eight and said, Tamsin, the count is wrong, here is the true one — the Gull would have had a part in a hundred more carry for eleven years, and the Company would have been eleven years richer, and when I came asking for a bell for a platform full of people they would have had eleven years of reasons to say yes."
She turned round.

"That is the regret," she said. "Not the theft. The theft was arithmetic. The regret is that I had a true thing and I kept it, and everything that happened afterwards happened in the space where that thing should have been."
Sol thought about that for the rest of the spring, and then for a long time after, and it settled into the shape her life took.

She wrote the interval up. That was the whole of her answer, and it looked like nothing: eleven pages, in plain words, with Dov's figures in an appendix, describing how to find the true interval of any bell by ear and by frame, and how to teach the lean to a hand who cannot feel the tenth. She sent copies to the four ships on the run, to the Bellwrights' Company, to the Foundry, and — because Halloway insisted, and Halloway was right about everything except people — to the commission at Antrell, who filed it.

The Cormorant's bell-master wrote back a letter of four lines that Sol kept in the tally for the rest of her career. It said that they had tried the lean, that it worked, that their coal was down two per cent in a month, and that if Miss Ferrant ever came aboard the Cormorant she would find that nobody there would let her pay for anything ever again.

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Three: Recast

blocks.c: Chapter Twenty-Three: Recast
They poured the new Ninth in Fourthmonth, on a clear morning, at the Foundry on the north face of the ridge, and everyone came.
Sol had not understood, until she stood in that yard, how much of a bell is a decision.

She had spent three years thinking of the Ninth as a fact — a thing that was simply there, like a mast or a rib, that had always been the shape it was. But a bell is nothing except a series of choices made by people, most of them in about four seconds: how much tin; how hot; how fast the metal runs; whether the mould is dry enough or merely dry. Get any of it wrong and you have eleven hundred pounds of expensive scrap and a shed full of people not looking at each other.

Ottring explained the whole of it to Beriah Okonkwo, who was fourteen and had come up from Kettlemouth on the strength of a letter from a bell-master, and who asked so many questions that Ottring eventually made her hold the tally-board and write the answers down, which is how apprenticeships have always started.

Master Ottring was eighty-one and had refused to retire on the grounds that nobody else in the yard could be trusted with a melt. She had the old Ninth broken up and weighed and put back in the crucible, because a recast bell is a rare thing and a bell recast from its own metal is rarer, and because — she said, to a shed full of people who had come to watch — a bell that has held eight hundred tons and four hundred and eleven souls for forty-one years has earned the right to go on doing it.
Kerrin came up the Low Stair for the first time in eleven years to stand in the yard. Pel came with her and spent the whole day looking at things.
Roake stood at the front with her hand flat on the shed wall, feeling the furnace through the timber.

Dov had built something. Of course he had. It was a frame of wire and iron rods, and it stood beside the mould, and when Ottring's crew broke the plug and the metal went in with that enormous soft roar, the frame hummed, and Roake — who could not hear the pour, or the roar, or the cheer that went up from four hundred people in a foundry yard — felt every bit of it come up through the wall into her palm and she put her head back and laughed out loud.
Sol had the last of it, because Ottring made her.

"Girl. Come here. This is the alloy tray. When it's cooling you can put a thing in the crown-mould and it goes in the bell, and every foundry in the world says it's superstition and every foundry in the world does it. What are you putting in?"
Sol had thought about this for four months.

She put in a hammer-lanyard: eleven inches of spliced cord, the splice done by a woman with hands broken often enough to have opinions about the weather, cut from the lanyard Roake had been mending in the cubby at half past four in the morning on the night Sol first came to her with a story nobody would believe.
"That'll burn," said Ottring.
"I know."
"Burns to about nothing. A smudge of carbon in eleven hundred pounds of bronze. Won't change the note by a hair; won't change anything at all."
"I know," said Sol.
Ottring looked at her for a moment.
"Good," she said. "That's the correct reason. Put it in."

They hung the new Ninth in Sixthmonth. Ottring tuned it herself over nine days, taking metal off the inside of the rim with a lathe, four ounces at a time, listening after each pass with her cheek against the metal.

Sol was allowed to listen on the fourth day and the seventh and the ninth, and on the fourth day the bell was flat and sullen and sounded like an apology, and on the seventh it had begun to open, and on the ninth she put her cheek to the cold bronze and heard, in the long tail under the note, something she had been listening for without knowing it since a night on a gallery eleven months before.

It was not the old Ninth. She had half expected it to be, and had been braced to pretend. It was a different bell with the same voice — the way a daughter has her mother's laugh and none of her opinions.

On the ninth day she came out into the yard, wiped her hands, and said: "Four and one. Not four. If any hand of yours rings that bell at four flat I will come up on the ferry personally and I will not be pleasant."
"Yes, ma'am," said Sol.
"Who's ringing it in?"
There was a pause. Everyone in the yard knew what a ringing-in was, and everyone knew that it belonged, by four hundred years of custom, to the bell-master of the ship.
Tamsin Roake, who had been reading lips all morning, put her hand on Sol's shoulder and pushed her forward, hard enough to stagger her.
"Bosun—"

Roake handed her the slate. She had written it out in advance, which meant she had known for weeks, which meant she had been waiting for the day with the ordinary patience of a woman who had waited eleven years for one nod on a wharf.
Bell-master of the Meridian Gull, from the ringing-in. Papers signed and lodged at Antrell. Marn countersigned. Kerrin countersigned, which cost her a great deal and which I made her do anyway.
You will be told you are too young. You are. Everyone is. I was twenty-nine and I rang four flat for twenty-two years.

I will be aboard as ship's carpenter's mate, which is a real job and which I can do with my hands, and if you ever again put a hush plate in front of me and ask me not to use it I will throw you off this ship myself.
Sol stood in a foundry yard holding a slate and could not see any of it for about eleven seconds.
Then she wiped her face on her sleeve, because four hundred people were watching, and took the hammer.

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Four: Bell-Master of the Meridian Gull

blocks.c: Chapter Twenty-Four: Bell-Master of the Meridian Gull
The third watch belongs to Sol Ferrant, and the third watch belongs to nobody, which is much the same thing.

She climbs the bell ladder at ten minutes to four with the rope callus on her right palm itching the way it always does before a round, and she counts the rungs, because counting is free. Nineteen rungs from the galley deck to the ring gallery. Nineteen going up, nineteen coming down, and in between, nine bells and four hundred and eleven passengers, and — for the last eleven minutes of the down leg, four miles north of the Quiet — two hundred and nineteen more, four hundred feet below, in a town that has to be rung.

There is a new hand this season. Her name is Beriah Okonkwo, she is fourteen, she is from Kettlemouth, and she has the sort of ear that makes Sol's stomach turn over with recognition. She follows Sol up the ladder and counts the rungs out loud, which is a thing Sol has told her not to do and will keep telling her not to do for about a year, until she starts doing it silently, which is what happened to Sol.
At the top the world goes quiet in the way high places do.
"Walk the line," says Sol.
"Bosun says that's superstition."

"Bosun is deaf as a post and reads lips, and I notice you waited until she was below to say that." Sol takes the hammer off its hook. "Yes. It's superstition. Walk it anyway. There's nine bells and each one of them has broken somebody's heart at some point, and you will do a better job of ringing a thing you have touched."
They walk it. Keel. Ladder. Kestrel. Quarrel. Mother. Lantern. Thimble. Widow.

And at the stern, small and high and bright, and eight months old, and made out of a forty-one-year-old bell with eleven inches of somebody's spliced cord burned to a smudge of carbon somewhere in the crown: the Ninth.
"Interval," says Sol.
"Four and one."
"What's the one?"
"A tenth of a beat."
"How do you count a tenth of a beat?"
Beriah, who has been asked this four times and has never once got it right, says: "You don't count it. You lean on it."
Sol turns round. "Who told you that?"

"You did. Last month. You said counting gets you the four and leaning gets you the one, and if I ever work out how to say that properly I'm to write it down, because nobody in four hundred years has managed it."
"Huh," says Sol. "That's good. I don't remember saying that."
"You'd been awake for two days."
"That'll be why it's good."
She hands over the hammer, because that is how it is done and always has been: the new hand rings the eight and the bell-master rings the ninth, until one day she doesn't.
"Keel," says Sol. "In your own time. Don't look at me, look at the bell. It doesn't care that you're nervous and neither do I."
Beriah rings Keel, and it is a fraction hard, and the note comes off the sound-bow with a burr on it that a passenger would never hear in a hundred crossings.
"Softer. You're hitting it like it owes you money."

Ladder. Better. Kestrel, Quarrel — both clean. Mother takes her breath and says everything at once, and Beriah laughs out loud in the middle of a round, which is a hanging offence in four hundred years of custom and which Sol lets go, because she did exactly the same thing at fourteen and Roake had let it go.
Lantern. Thimble. Widow, sour and reliable.
Eight bells, rung true by a girl who came aboard nine weeks ago and could not hold a count for four strikes together.
"Well?" says Beriah, who is trying extremely hard to sound as though she does not care.
"That was a round," says Sol. "Give it here."

She rings the round again from the top, because a chapter of a ship's day is not finished until the bell-master has put her own hands on all nine of it, and because the round is not a ceremony, it is a job.

Keel, low and enormous, the sound going out and down and out again. Ladder, four and one later. Kestrel. Quarrel. Mother, who takes a full breath to decide to speak and then says everything at once. Lantern. Thimble. Widow, sour and reliable.
Sol walks the last six paces to the stern with the whole ship humming under her boots, and she lifts the hammer to the Ninth, and she strikes it, and it rings beautifully.
And then she holds, and counts nine, and waits.

And from four hundred feet below the keel line, out of the dark, up through the frames and the plating and the soles of two pairs of boots, comes the twin: a bell rung by a young man called Pel who is twenty-one now and has a daughter, in a town with a school and a chandler and a chapel that used to be two chapels, on a frame with new iron in the north side and four years of good hard hammering left to do.
Beriah Okonkwo, fourteen years old, on her fourth night on the ring gallery, feels it come up through her feet and says, "Oh."
"Yes," says Sol Ferrant.

She does not explain it. There will be time for the explaining: the pour book, the eleven years, the cupboard in the forward hold, a woman with a handcart on a wet Tuesday, a purser who would not write nil, a bosun who cannot hear a bell and marks them full or thin by feel and is never wrong. Beriah will get all of it, in pieces, over about four years, in the order things are actually learned, which is never the order they happened.
Tonight she gets the sound.
"That's — it's not ours."
"No," says the bell-master of the Meridian Gull, and hangs the hammer back on its hook, and picks up the tally, and hands it to her. "Write it down."
